ミラー指数.desc: Sets of integers that describe planes and directions in a crystal. For a plane, the reciprocals of its intercepts on the axes are reduced to the smallest integer ratio and written (hkl); a direction is written [uvw].

about.h: Finding the indices of a plane
about.p: The Miller indices of a plane are found by the following steps. First, read the points where the plane meets the crystal axes x, y and z (the intercepts) in units of the lattice parameters a, b and c. Next, take the reciprocal of each, clear fractions to get the smallest integer ratio, and write the result in parentheses as (hkl). For example, if the intercepts are 1, 2 and ∞, the reciprocals are 1, 1/2 and 0, giving (210). A plane parallel to an axis has an infinite intercept on it, so that index is 0. Negative intercepts are shown with a bar over the number. If the plane passes through the origin, move the origin to a neighboring lattice point before reading the intercepts.

about.h: Direction indices and families of equivalent planes
about.p: Direction indices are the coordinates of a point reached by moving from the origin in that direction, reduced to the smallest integer ratio and written in square brackets as [uvw]. In cubic crystals many planes are equivalent by symmetry; (100), (010), (001) and so on are written together in braces as {100}, and equivalent directions together in angle brackets as <100>. Cubic crystals have the convenient property that the [hkl] direction is exactly perpendicular to the (hkl) plane, so angles between planes can also be found from dot products of directions. Note that this property does not hold in general for tetragonal or hexagonal crystals.

The interplanar spacing of a cubic crystal is calculated as d = a/√(h² + k² + l²). Planes with larger indices have smaller spacings, and their XRD peaks appear at higher angles. Depending on the arrangement of atoms in the unit cell, however, diffraction from some planes cancels out and does not appear. In BCC only planes with h + k + l even diffract, and in FCC only planes with h, k and l all even or all odd (the extinction rules). Correctly indexing the peaks is the starting point for determining lattice parameters and identifying phases.

For hexagonal crystals such as HCP, Miller–Bravais indices (hkil) are widely used, with three axes a₁, a₂ and a₃ at 120° to each other in the basal plane plus the c axis. The relation i = −(h + k) holds, and the advantage is that equivalent planes have the same pattern of numbers. For example, the basal plane is (0001) and prism planes take the form {10-10}. These indices appear constantly in materials and device specifications, for wafer orientations, the orientation of epitaxial films and the notation of slip systems, so it pays to be able to picture a plane's orientation from its indices.

faq.q: What do the different kinds of brackets mean in Miller indices?
faq.a: (hkl) denotes a single plane, {hkl} a family of planes equivalent by symmetry, [uvw] a single direction, and <uvw> a family of equivalent directions. The slip system of FCC, for example, is written {111}<110>.

faq.q: How do I write a negative intercept?
faq.a: A negative index obtained after taking the reciprocal is shown with a bar over the number. In plain text a minus sign is sometimes used instead, as in (1-10).

faq.q: Are the (200) and (100) planes the same plane?
faq.a: They have the same orientation, but (200) denotes a set of planes with half the spacing of (100). In XRD, the second-order reflection from (100) is treated as a first-order reflection from the (200) planes with half the spacing.

面心立方格子.desc: A crystal structure (FCC) with atoms at the corners of the cube and at the center of each face. The unit cell contains 4 atoms; the coordination number is 12 and the packing factor about 0.74. Examples include Cu, Al and Ni.

体心立方格子.desc: A crystal structure (BCC) with atoms at the corners and the center of the cube. The unit cell contains 2 atoms; the coordination number is 8 and the packing factor about 0.68. Examples include α-iron, Cr and W.

六方最密構造.desc: A crystal structure (HCP) formed by stacking close-packed planes in an ABAB… sequence. The coordination number is 12 and the ideal c/a is about 1.633. Examples include Mg, Ti and Zn.

原子充填率.desc: The fraction of the unit-cell volume occupied by atoms, treating atoms as hard spheres. About 0.52 for SC, about 0.68 for BCC and about 0.74 for FCC and HCP.

転位.desc: A defect in which the arrangement of atoms in a crystal is disturbed along a line. Metals deform plastically as dislocations move on slip planes. There are edge, screw and mixed dislocations.

about.p: The theoretical shear strength needed to shift an entire plane of atoms at once is estimated at about one tenth of the shear modulus, yet real metals yield at stresses a thousandth of that or less. Dislocations explain this large gap. With a dislocation present, there is no need to break atomic bonds all at once; the crystal slips by rearranging bonds a few at a time near the dislocation line, much as moving a ruck in a carpet shifts the whole carpet. How easily a metal deforms plastically is therefore determined by how easily its dislocations move.

The type of dislocation is determined by the relation between the Burgers vector b, which gives the magnitude and direction of slip, and the direction of the dislocation line. An edge dislocation has the form of an inserted extra half-plane of atoms, with b perpendicular to the line. In a screw dislocation the atomic planes connect like a spiral staircase, with b parallel to the line. Most dislocations are mixed dislocations combining the two. An edge dislocation has a unique slip plane and, at high temperature, can climb up or down by absorbing or emitting vacancies. A screw dislocation can cross-slip onto another slip plane.

Most strengthening methods for metals work by obstructing dislocation motion. Solid-solution strengthening stops dislocations with the strain fields of solute atoms, precipitation hardening with fine precipitates, grain refinement with grain boundaries, and work hardening with entanglement of dislocations among themselves. Cold working raises the dislocation density from about 10¹⁰ m⁻² to about 10¹⁵ m⁻², increasing strength while lowering ductility. Conversely, when recovery and recrystallization occur during annealing, the dislocation density falls and softness and ductility return.

Dislocations can be observed directly by TEM as lines of diffraction contrast caused by strain. At a surface, etching forms etch pits where dislocations meet the surface, and counting their density gives the dislocation density. Silicon wafers are made essentially dislocation-free, but if dislocations are introduced during processing, for example by thermal stress, they increase leakage current and become sites for precipitation of metal impurities. When a film with a different lattice parameter is grown, misfit dislocations form at the interface to relax the strain, and threading dislocations may remain in the film.

faq.q: How do dislocations multiply?
faq.a: During plastic deformation they multiply by mechanisms such as the Frank–Read source, in which a dislocation pinned at both ends bows out and generates loop after loop. The dislocation density therefore increases as working proceeds, causing work hardening.

faq.q: How are dislocations and the Burgers vector related?
faq.a: If you make a closed circuit around a dislocation, a closure failure remains compared with a perfect crystal. This is the Burgers vector, which gives the amount and direction by which the crystal is displaced when the dislocation passes.

faq.q: Why do dislocations move with difficulty in ceramics?
faq.a: In ionic bonding, slip must avoid bringing ions of the same sign together, and in covalent bonding the bonds are strongly directional, so slip systems are limited and the Peierls stress is large. At room temperature ceramics therefore fracture in a brittle manner before deforming plastically.

バーガースベクトル.desc: The vector giving the closure failure of a circuit taken around a dislocation. For a perfect dislocation in FCC it is (a/2)<110>. It determines the type and energy of the dislocation.

拡散係数.desc: The coefficient D expressing how readily atoms diffuse, in units of m²/s. It depends on temperature in the Arrhenius form D = D₀exp(−Q/RT).

about.p: The diffusion coefficient D is the proportionality constant in Fick's first law, J = −D(dC/dx), that links the concentration gradient to the flow of atoms (the flux). Its unit is m²/s (cm²/s is also common), and the larger it is, the faster atoms spread. A rough distance over which atoms spread in time t is √(Dt). For example, with D = 10⁻¹¹ m²/s, atoms spread about 0.2 mm in one hour (3600 s). It is the basic quantity for estimating carburized case depths, dopant diffusion depths and the growth of reaction layers in solder joints.

about.h: Temperature dependence and the Arrhenius plot
about.p: The diffusion coefficient depends exponentially on temperature, D = D₀exp(−Q/RT). Q is the activation energy needed for an atom to jump to a neighboring site, and D₀ is a constant that includes the vibration frequency and jump distance. Plotting ln D against 1/T (an Arrhenius plot) gives a straight line, and Q is obtained from its slope −Q/R. The larger Q, the stronger the effect of temperature, and a difference of a few tens of degrees can change the diffusion rate several times over. In calculations, it is essential to convert temperatures to absolute temperature.

about.h: The mechanism changes the order of magnitude
about.p: Small atoms such as carbon, nitrogen and hydrogen in iron move by interstitial diffusion, jumping between interstitial sites, so their diffusion coefficients are large. Substitutional atoms diffuse by the vacancy mechanism, moving only when a vacancy arrives next to them; the activation energy also includes the vacancy formation energy, so diffusion is far slower. In addition, diffusion along grain boundaries, surfaces and dislocations, where the atomic arrangement is disordered, has a lower activation energy and can dominate over lattice diffusion at low temperatures. This is why grain boundary diffusion stands out in polycrystalline thin films.

When different atoms diffuse into each other, as when two metals are bonded, the diffusion coefficient of each kind of atom (the intrinsic diffusion coefficient) must be distinguished from the interdiffusion coefficient that describes the overall change in concentration. The difference between them shows up as marker movement and void formation through the Kirkendall effect. In practice, the diffusion coefficient at the treatment temperature is calculated from literature values of D₀ and Q, and the concentration profile is predicted with the error-function solution. Values differ between data sources, so it is safer to compare several before use.

faq.q: Why is the unit of the diffusion coefficient m²/s?
faq.a: In J = −D(dC/dx), the flux J has units of (amount)/(m²·s) and the concentration gradient (amount)/m⁴, so D has units of m²/s. This is also consistent with √(Dt) being a length.

faq.q: How many degrees must the temperature be raised to double the diffusion coefficient?
faq.a: It depends on the activation energy and the temperature. Solve ln 2 = (Q/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂); for example, with Q = 150 kJ/mol and T₁ = 1200 K, raising the temperature by about 58 K roughly doubles the diffusion coefficient.

faq.q: How are the diffusion coefficient and the diffusion length related?
faq.a: A rough diffusion distance in time t is √(Dt) (or 2√(Dt), depending on the definition). The distance is proportional to the square root of time, so doubling the depth takes four times as long.

フィックの法則.desc: The basic laws of diffusion. The first law states that the flux is proportional to the concentration gradient, J = −D(dC/dx); the second gives the change of concentration with time, ∂C/∂t = D(∂²C/∂x²).

空孔.desc: A point defect in which an atom is missing from a lattice site. Its equilibrium concentration rises with temperature as exp(−Q/kT), and vacancies carry the diffusion of substitutional atoms.

破壊靭性.desc: The ability of a cracked material to resist fracture. It is expressed as the critical value of the stress intensity factor, K_IC (in MPa·√m), and fracture is judged by comparing it with K = Yσ√(πa).

about.h: The stress intensity factor and the fracture condition
about.p: The intensity of stress at a crack tip is expressed by the stress intensity factor K = Yσ√(πa). σ is the remote stress, a is the crack length (the depth for a surface crack, half the length for an internal crack), and Y is a factor determined by the shapes of the crack and component. When K reaches a critical value for the material, the crack propagates suddenly and fracture occurs; this critical value is called the fracture toughness. Its unit is MPa·√m, notable for containing both stress and crack length. It lets you compare numerically not just strength but resistance to cracks.

Fracture toughness values change with plate thickness. Thin plates are close to plane stress with a large plastic zone at the crack tip, so the apparent value is high; thick plates are in plane strain, and the value drops and levels off at a constant minimum. This value is the plane-strain fracture toughness K_IC, where the subscript I denotes loading that opens the crack (mode I). K_IC can be treated as a material constant and is a conservative value for design. Typical values are about 50–150 MPa·√m for structural steels (lower for higher-strength grades), about 20–45 for aluminum alloys, about 3–5 for alumina and below 1 (about 0.7–0.8) for soda-lime glass.

In general, raising strength by heat treatment or other means tends to lower fracture toughness. The higher the strength, the smaller the crack that can be tolerated, and since the critical crack length is proportional to (K_IC/σ)², the effect is large even when the working stress is the same fraction of the strength. Aircraft and pressure vessels therefore select materials for toughness as well as strength. In ceramics, toughness is raised by measures such as transformation toughening in zirconia and crack bridging by fibers or particles. In metals, grain refinement and reducing inclusions improve toughness.

In damage-tolerant design, you assume the largest crack that nondestructive inspection might miss and check that K at the working stress stays below K_IC. Combining this with the Paris law for fatigue crack growth rate, you estimate the number of cycles for the crack to reach its critical length and set the inspection interval. For highly ductile materials with large plastic zones, K is hard to apply, so elastic–plastic fracture mechanics parameters such as the J-integral and the crack-tip opening displacement (CTOD) are used. Which parameter to use is judged from the ductility of the material and the dimensions of the component.

faq.q: How does fracture toughness differ from impact energy (Charpy absorbed energy)?
faq.a: Charpy impact energy is the energy needed to break a notched specimen; it is convenient for comparing materials and evaluating the ductile-to-brittle transition, but it is not a value that can be used directly in design. Fracture toughness is a material constant that lets you predict fracture quantitatively from crack size and stress.

faq.q: Where does the unit of K_IC, MPa·√m, come from?
faq.a: In K = Yσ√(πa), σ is in MPa and a in m, giving MPa·√m. Y and π are dimensionless.

faq.q: What is the fracture toughness of ceramics?
faq.a: About 3–5 MPa·√m for alumina, about 5–8 for silicon nitride and about 6–10 for partially stabilized zirconia, from a few tens of times to a few times lower than metals. Ceramics therefore fracture easily even from small flaws, and their strength scatters widely.

0.2%耐力.desc: For materials without a distinct yield point, the stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.2% after unloading. It is found where a line parallel to the elastic line, offset by 0.2% strain, meets the stress–strain curve.

ヤング率.desc: The ratio of stress to strain in the elastic region, E = σ/ε. It is set by interatomic bonding: about 200 GPa for steel and about 70 GPa for aluminum, and it hardly changes with heat treatment.

疲労限度.desc: The stress amplitude below which a material effectively no longer fails under cyclic loading. It often appears at around 10⁶–10⁷ cycles in carbon steels but is not distinct in aluminum alloys.

クリープ.desc: Deformation that progresses over time under a constant load. It becomes significant above roughly 0.4 times the melting point (in absolute temperature) and passes through primary, secondary (steady-state) and tertiary stages before rupture.

てこの規則.desc: A rule for finding the mass fraction of each phase in a two-phase region of a phase diagram from ratios of distances along the tie line. The fraction of a phase is proportional to the distance from the alloy composition to the opposite phase.

about.p: Consider an alloy in a two-phase region of a binary phase diagram. If you draw a horizontal line (the tie line) at that temperature, its two ends meet the boundaries of the two phases, and the compositions at those intersections are the compositions of the two phases. The overall alloy composition C₀ lies somewhere along the tie line; because the compositions of the two phases are fixed by temperature alone, changing the alloy composition does not change the phase compositions, only the proportions of the phases. The lever rule gives these proportions and is derived from the overall alloy composition and the conservation of mass of each component.

With Cα the composition of the α phase and C_L that of the other phase (the liquid, say), the mass fraction of liquid is W_L = (Cα − C₀)/(Cα − C_L) and the mass fraction of α is Wα = (C₀ − C_L)/(Cα − C_L). The name comes from the resemblance to the balance of a lever (seesaw): the fraction of a phase is proportional to the distance from the alloy composition to the composition of the opposite phase. A common mistake is to take the distance on the same side. You can check the result by confirming that the two fractions sum to 1. With compositions in wt% you get mass fractions; in at%, fractions by number of atoms.

In eutectic and eutectoid systems it is important to distinguish the fractions of phases from those of microconstituents. For example, a hypoeutectoid steel just below 727 °C has two phases, ferrite and cementite, but two microconstituents, proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite. The fraction of proeutectoid ferrite is found with the lever rule in the α + γ region just above 727 °C, while the fraction of all ferrite as a phase is found in the α + Fe₃C region. Being conscious of which tie line at which temperature you are using prevents mix-ups.

about.h: Relation to real microstructures and caveats
about.p: The lever rule assumes equilibrium. With rapid cooling, as in real casting, diffusion in the solid cannot keep up and segregation remains, so fractions and compositions do not match the calculation. Even so, measuring the area fraction of pearlite in the micrograph of a slowly cooled steel lets you back-calculate its approximate carbon content. Also, when the two phases differ greatly in density, mass fractions do not match the area (volume) fractions seen in a microscope, so convert between mass and volume fractions using the density of each phase as needed.

faq.q: Can the lever rule be used when three phases coexist?
faq.a: In a binary system three phases coexist only at invariant points such as the eutectic temperature, where the fractions are not uniquely determined. Find them with the lever rule in the two-phase regions just above or just below the eutectic temperature.

faq.q: Should I calculate in wt% or at%?
faq.a: If you calculate in the same units as the phase diagram, wt% gives mass fractions and at% gives fractions by number of atoms. The important thing is not to mix units partway through.

faq.q: Why is the distance to the opposite side used?
faq.a: Because the closer the alloy composition is to the composition of one phase, the more of that phase there should be. Solving the conservation of total solute, C₀ = Wα·Cα + W_L·C_L, confirms that the result is the ratio of distances to the opposite side.

ギブスの相律.desc: The rule F = C − P + 2 giving the number of degrees of freedom F at equilibrium from the number of components C and the number of phases P. For condensed systems at constant pressure, F = C − P + 1 is used.

共晶反応.desc: A reaction in which two solid phases crystallize simultaneously from the liquid on cooling, L → α + β. In a binary system it occurs at a fixed temperature and composition and produces eutectic structures such as lamellae.

共析反応.desc: A reaction in which two solid phases form simultaneously from one solid phase on cooling. In steel, γ → α + Fe₃C occurs at 0.76 wt% C and 727 °C, producing pearlite.

パーライト.desc: The microstructure formed by the eutectoid reaction in steel, with alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite. The faster the cooling, the finer the lamellar spacing and the harder the pearlite.

マルテンサイト.desc: The microstructure formed by a diffusionless, shear-type transformation when austenite is quenched. In steel it is body-centered tetragonal, supersaturated with carbon, and very hard.

about.p: When steel is cooled from the austenite region faster than the critical cooling rate, carbon atoms have no time to diffuse and form cementite. Instead, a shear-type transformation occurs in which iron atoms shift cooperatively by small amounts, and FCC austenite changes into body-centered tetragonal (BCT) martensite supersaturated with carbon. Atoms move less than an interatomic distance, and the transformation proceeds at nearly the speed of sound. The composition does not change across the transformation, and a distinctive feature is that the amount transformed is set by the temperature reached, not by the holding time.

The martensitic transformation starts at the Ms temperature during cooling, progresses as the temperature falls, and is nearly complete at the Mf temperature. Ms and Mf fall as the carbon and alloy contents increase, and in high-carbon steels Mf is below room temperature, so retained austenite that has not transformed remains. Retained austenite transforms over time and causes dimensional changes, so precision parts are given a subzero treatment, cooling below 0 °C. The volume expansion and temperature differences during quenching also cause quench cracking and distortion.

about.h: The source of hardness and tempering
about.p: The hardness of martensite is determined mainly by its carbon content; the large lattice strain from supersaturated carbon and the high dislocation density strongly obstruct dislocation motion. On the other hand, martensite is very brittle, so it is normally tempered before use. During tempering, the supersaturated carbon precipitates as fine carbides and internal stresses relax, so hardness falls but toughness recovers substantially. Low-temperature tempering is used for tools and high-temperature tempering for shafts and gears (combined with the preceding quench, this is called quenching and tempering), giving a combination of hardness and toughness suited to the application.

The martensitic transformation is not unique to steel. In Ni-Ti alloys, the martensitic transformation and its reverse give the shape memory effect and superelasticity, used in medical wires and actuators. The tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation of zirconia is also martensitic and is exploited in transformation toughening. All share the same mechanism of cooperative atomic shifts without diffusion, and the crystallography of the transformation determines macroscopic properties. Transformation temperatures vary greatly with alloy composition, so composition control is important.

faq.q: Why is martensite hard?
faq.a: Because carbon dissolved in supersaturation greatly distorts the lattice, and the transformation also introduces many dislocations and twins, making dislocations very hard to move. Its hardness is determined mainly by the carbon content.

faq.q: Does quenching always produce martensite?
faq.a: If the cooling rate is slower than the critical cooling rate, pearlite or bainite forms along the way. The centers of thick sections cool slowly, so alloy steels with high hardenability or quenchants with high cooling power are used.

faq.q: What is retained austenite?
faq.a: In steels whose Mf is below room temperature, it is austenite that remains untransformed after quenching. It transforms over time and changes dimensions, so it is reduced by subzero treatment or tempering.

焼戻し.desc: A heat treatment that reheats quenched steel to a temperature below the A1 temperature (727 °C). It restores toughness and reduces internal stresses at the cost of some hardness.

析出硬化.desc: Strengthening by dispersing fine precipitates through solution treatment, quenching and aging, so that they obstruct dislocation motion. Used in alloys such as Al-Cu; aging too long causes softening by overaging.

ホール・ペッチの関係.desc: The relation σy = σ₀ + k/√d in which the yield stress increases in inverse proportion to the square root of the grain size d. Grain boundaries obstruct dislocation motion, so finer grains give higher strength.

焼入れ性.desc: The depth to which martensite can be obtained by quenching (how readily a steel hardens). It increases when alloying elements such as Mn, Cr and Mo shift the nose of the TTT diagram to longer times.

焼結.desc: The process of heating a powder compact at a high temperature below the melting point so that the particles bond and the compact densifies. The driving force is the reduction in surface energy.

ワイブル係数.desc: The parameter m of the Weibull distribution that expresses how small the scatter in strength is. The larger it is, the smaller the scatter: about 5–20 for ceramics and several tens or more for metals.

圧電効果.desc: The phenomenon in which applying stress produces polarization and, conversely, applying an electric field produces deformation. It occurs in crystals without a center of symmetry; quartz and PZT are used in sensors and resonators.

ペロブスカイト構造.desc: An ABO₃ crystal structure in which the B-site cation sits at the center of an oxygen octahedron (coordination number 6) and the A-site cation in the space between octahedra (coordination number 12). BaTiO₃ is an example.

変態強化.desc: The mechanism in partially stabilized zirconia by which stress at a crack tip transforms tetragonal to monoclinic, and the accompanying volume expansion closes the crack and raises toughness.

ガラス転移温度.desc: The temperature at which molecular or atomic motion in an amorphous substance or the amorphous regions of a polymer freezes, switching between the glassy and rubbery (supercooled liquid) states. Written Tg.

about.p: As a liquid or polymer melt is cooled, molecular rearrangement gradually slows. When rearrangement can no longer keep up with cooling, the structure freezes in place and the material enters the glassy state, behaving like a solid. The temperature at which this switch occurs is the glass transition temperature Tg, where the temperature dependence of specific volume, heat capacity and thermal expansion coefficient shows a kink. In polymers, segmental motion, in which several units of the backbone move together, becomes active above Tg, giving a soft, rubbery state.

about.h: How it differs from the melting point
about.p: The melting point Tm is the temperature of a thermodynamic phase transition at which crystals melt, and it has a definite value. Tg, on the other hand, is a kinetic phenomenon determined by the balance between relaxation time and observation time, and its value changes with cooling rate, heating rate and measurement frequency. The faster the cooling, the higher the temperature at which the structure freezes, and the higher Tg. Crystalline polymers have both a melting point Tm for the crystalline regions and a Tg for the amorphous regions; Tg is always lower than Tm, often by a ratio of about 0.5–0.8 in absolute temperature. Amorphous polymers have no Tm, only a Tg.

The harder it is for chains to move, the higher Tg. Polymers with stiff structures such as aromatic rings in the backbone, bulky side groups, strong interchain interactions or many crosslinks have high Tg: about 150 °C for polycarbonate and about 100 °C for polystyrene. Conversely, polyethylene and silicone rubber, with flexible backbones, have Tg far below room temperature. Plasticizers and moisture enter between chains, increase free volume and lower Tg. In epoxy resins, the drop in Tg on moisture absorption is a reliability concern.

Tg is measured from the stepwise change in heat capacity in DSC, the kink in the expansion coefficient in thermomechanical analysis (TMA), and the sharp drop in storage modulus or the peak in the loss tangent tanδ in dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA). Even for the same material, the value can differ by more than 10 °C depending on the method, the heating rate and, for DMA, the frequency, so check the measurement conditions when comparing data. For semiconductor encapsulants and substrate resins, the expansion coefficient and modulus change greatly above Tg, so its relation to temperatures such as reflow matters.

faq.q: Above the glass transition temperature, does a polymer become a liquid?
faq.a: An amorphous polymer first enters a rubbery region above Tg and begins to flow as the temperature rises further. Crosslinked thermosetting resins remain rubbery above Tg and do not flow.

faq.q: Why do DSC and DMA give different Tg values?
faq.a: Tg is a kinetic phenomenon, so its value changes with the time scale of the measurement. The DMA tanδ peak often comes out higher than the DSC midpoint value, so state which definition is used when comparing.

faq.q: Is the Tg of glass the same thing as the Tg of polymers?
faq.a: Both are glass transitions caused by the freezing of structure, and the mechanism is the same. The ranges of values differ widely, however: several hundred °C for silicate glasses versus roughly −100 °C to 200 °C for polymers.

結晶化度.desc: The fraction of a crystalline polymer occupied by crystalline regions. It is determined from density, the heat of fusion by DSC, XRD and so on; higher crystallinity raises density and modulus but lowers transparency.

粘弾性.desc: Behavior that combines properties of an elastic solid and of a viscous fluid. In polymers it appears as stress relaxation and creep and depends on time and temperature.

熱硬化性樹脂.desc: A resin that forms a three-dimensional network by a curing reaction and does not melt when heated after curing. Examples include epoxy and phenolic resins.

複合則.desc: Expressions that estimate the properties of a composite from the properties and volume fractions of its constituents. Along the fibers, the isostrain form E = VfEf + VmEm applies; perpendicular to them, the isostress form is used as an approximation.

マティーセンの規則.desc: The empirical rule that the resistivity of a metal is the sum of a temperature-dependent component due to lattice vibrations and a temperature-independent component due to impurities and defects.

キュリー温度.desc: The temperature at which a ferromagnet (or ferroelectric) loses its spontaneous magnetization (or polarization); above it the material is paramagnetic. About 770 °C for iron and about 358 °C for nickel.

保磁力.desc: The strength of the reverse magnetic field needed to bring the magnetization (or flux density) of a magnetized material back to zero. Materials with small coercivity are soft magnetic, and those with large coercivity hard magnetic.

軟磁性材料.desc: A magnetic material with small coercivity and low hysteresis loss, such as electrical steel, ferrites and amorphous alloys, used for transformer and motor cores.

間接遷移型半導体.desc: A semiconductor whose conduction band minimum and valence band maximum occur at different crystal momenta. Radiative recombination requires a phonon, so emission efficiency is low. Silicon and germanium are examples.

臨界核半径.desc: The nucleus radius above which growth becomes the more stable path in nucleation. For a spherical nucleus, r* = −2γ/ΔGv, which becomes smaller as the undercooling increases.

ストランスキー・クラスタノフ成長.desc: A thin-film growth mode in which, after layer-by-layer growth of a few atomic layers, three-dimensional islands grow to relax the strain from lattice mismatch. It is used to make quantum dots.

熱応力.desc: Stress arising from a difference in thermal expansion. For a thin film on a substrate it is estimated as σ = EΔαΔT/(1 − ν); if the film's expansion coefficient is larger, the film is in tension after cooling.

オストワルド成長.desc: Coarsening in which small particles dissolve and disappear while large particles grow. The driving force is the curvature-dependent difference in solubility (the Gibbs–Thomson effect).

量子サイズ効果.desc: The effect by which energy levels become discrete and the band gap widens when particles or films become as small as the spatial extent of electron waves. It determines the emission color of quantum dots.

XRD(X線回折).desc: An analytical method that shines X-rays on a crystal and uses the angles and intensities of the diffracted X-rays to examine crystalline phases, lattice parameters, crystallite size, strain, texture and more.

about.p: XRD shines X-rays on a crystal, whose atomic spacings are comparable to the X-ray wavelength, and measures the diffracted X-rays that reinforce at angles satisfying Bragg's law. Peak positions give interplanar spacings and lattice parameters, and comparing the pattern with a database identifies the crystalline phases. Peak intensity ratios reveal texture and phase proportions, and peak widths reveal crystallite size and nonuniform strain. Amorphous materials show a broad halo instead of peaks, so XRD can also tell whether a material is crystalline or amorphous.

For powders and polycrystalline specimens, the basic method is θ-2θ measurement (Bragg–Brentano focusing), in which the specimen and detector rotate in step. In this geometry only planes parallel to the specimen surface are seen. For thin films, grazing-incidence measurements that send X-rays in at a shallow angle to probe only the near-surface region, rocking curves for examining texture and lattice tilt, and reciprocal space maps for examining the composition and strain of epitaxial films are used. Cu Kα radiation (wavelength about 0.154 nm) is the most commonly used X-ray source.

Precise lattice parameters obtained from peak positions allow estimates of solid-solution composition (Vegard's law) and residual stress (the sin²ψ method). Proportions of multiple phases are found by comparing peak intensities with standards or by Rietveld analysis, which fits the entire pattern to a calculation. Peak widths give crystallite size through the Scherrer equation, but instrumental broadening must be subtracted and the strain contribution separated. Accurate results require angle calibration and correction for specimen height displacement.

about.h: Use in failure analysis and quality control
about.p: In process work, XRD is used to confirm the phase and texture of deposited films (for example, identifying silicide phases or the (111) texture of Cu interconnects), to confirm crystallization by heat treatment, and to identify corrosion products and foreign matter. Detection generally requires a content of several percent or more and a certain volume, however, so XRD is poor at detecting tiny particles or trace phases. In such cases it is combined with micro-area XRD, electron diffraction in TEM, Raman spectroscopy and the like. A major advantage is that it is nondestructive, so it can be performed before other analyses.

faq.q: Can XRD be used for elemental analysis?
faq.a: XRD reveals crystal structure and cannot directly measure which elements are present. It can distinguish phases of the same elements with different structures, but elemental analysis calls for combining it with EDS, X-ray fluorescence or similar techniques.

faq.q: What happens when an amorphous film is measured by XRD?
faq.a: No sharp peaks appear, only a broad, gentle hump (a halo). If peaks appear after heat treatment, you can conclude that the film has crystallized.

faq.q: How deep does XRD probe?
faq.a: It depends on the material and the incidence angle, but in θ-2θ measurement it reaches several to several tens of micrometers in metals, and deeper still in materials of light elements. To measure only a thin film, use a grazing-incidence geometry.

SEM(走査電子顕微鏡).desc: A microscope that scans a finely focused electron beam across a specimen surface and detects the secondary and backscattered electrons emitted, to observe surface shape and differences in composition.

about.p: In an SEM, an electron beam accelerated to a few kV to about 30 kV is focused down to a few nanometers and scanned across the specimen surface. Displaying the amount of secondary or backscattered electrons emitted from each point as brightness, synchronized with the scan, forms the image. Compared with an optical microscope, the SEM has higher resolution (a few nanometers) and a much greater depth of focus, so rough fracture surfaces and powders can be observed in three-dimensional-looking images that are in focus throughout. Specimens must be conductive; insulators are coated with a thin film of metal or carbon or observed at low accelerating voltage.

Secondary electrons have low energies of 50 eV or less and can escape only from depths of a few nanometers, giving images of shape that strongly reflect surface tilt and edges. Backscattered electrons are incident electrons scattered back out by atoms; they have high energy and come from deeper regions. The backscattered yield increases with atomic number, giving compositional images in which regions of heavy elements are bright, and channeling contrast from crystal orientation can also be obtained. Comparing the two images lets you separate differences in shape from differences in composition.

When the electron beam strikes the specimen, characteristic X-rays with energies specific to each element are also emitted. Analyzing them by EDS or WDS gives elemental distributions as points, lines or maps. Note that characteristic X-rays come from a region of about 1 µm over which electrons spread, so the spatial resolution of elemental analysis is considerably worse than that of the image. In EBSD, the specimen is tilted steeply and the diffraction patterns of backscattered electrons are analyzed to map the orientation of each grain, the character of grain boundaries and the distribution of phases, useful for evaluating texture and recrystallization.

In failure analysis, fracture surfaces are examined to distinguish dimples of ductile fracture, striations of fatigue, cleavage facets of brittle fracture and so on, and to infer the cause of failure. For cross sections, a section is exposed by polishing, ion milling or FIB to examine voids in interconnects, intermetallic compounds in solder joints, film delamination and the like. For foreign particles, EDS confirms the elements present and helps identify their source. Conditions such as accelerating voltage and beam current are chosen with attention to charging, specimen damage and contamination (carbon deposition) by the electron beam.

faq.q: What is the difference between SEM and TEM?
faq.a: SEM observes surface shape and composition with electrons emitted from the surface, and the specimen may be thick. TEM observes the internal crystal structure and defects at the atomic level with electrons transmitted through a thin lamella.

faq.q: How are insulators observed in an SEM?
faq.a: Coat them with a few nanometers of gold, platinum or carbon to make them conductive, or use a low accelerating voltage that reduces charging, or a low-vacuum mode that admits gas into the specimen chamber.

faq.q: What is the resolution of an SEM?
faq.a: Instruments with field-emission electron guns reach around 1 nm, but it varies with the specimen, accelerating voltage and detector. The resolution of elemental analysis by EDS is considerably coarser and can be about 1 µm.

ブラッグの法則.desc: The condition 2d sinθ = nλ for diffraction to reinforce from crystal planes with spacing d. It is the basic equation for finding interplanar spacings from XRD peak angles.

about.p: Think of a crystal as a stack of parallel atomic planes with spacing d. When X-rays of wavelength λ strike the planes at an angle θ, the path difference between X-rays reflected from adjacent planes is 2d sinθ. When this difference is an integer multiple of the wavelength, nλ, the reflections from all planes line up in phase and reinforce. This is Bragg's law, 2d sinθ = nλ. θ is the angle between the planes and the X-rays, so the angle between the incident and diffracted X-rays is 2θ, which is normally plotted on the horizontal axis in XRD.

For example, with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) and planes with d = 0.2088 nm, sinθ = 0.15406/(2 × 0.2088) ≈ 0.369, so θ ≈ 21.7° and 2θ ≈ 43.3°. Common mistakes are confusing 2θ with θ and dropping the factor of 2 in the equation. Because sinθ cannot exceed 1, planes with d < λ/2 do not diffract, and shorter wavelengths allow more peaks to be measured. Higher-order reflections (n = 2 and above) are normally treated as first-order reflections from planes with spacing d/n and labeled with indices such as (200).

about.h: Use for cubic crystals and extinction rules
about.p: For cubic crystals the interplanar spacing is d = a/√(h² + k² + l²), so combining it with Bragg's law gives sin²θ = (λ²/4a²)(h² + k² + l²), and the ratios of sin²θ for the peaks reveal the sequence of h² + k² + l². Depending on the arrangement of atoms in the unit cell, however, diffraction from some planes cancels and disappears (the extinction rules). In BCC only planes with h + k + l even appear, and in FCC only planes with h, k and l all even or all odd; from these sequences the structure can be identified and the lattice parameter determined.

Bragg's law is a condition for wave interference, so it applies not only to X-rays but also to electron and neutron diffraction. In TEM electron diffraction, the electron wavelength is very short (about 0.0025 nm at 200 kV) and θ is small, about 1°, so sinθ ≈ θ is used to find interplanar spacings from the spacing of diffraction spots. The same principle is used in EBSD in the SEM, in WDS with its analyzing crystals, and in the spectrometers of X-ray fluorescence analysis, making it a common foundation for many materials analysis techniques.

faq.q: What is the difference between θ and 2θ in Bragg's law?
faq.a: θ is the angle between the crystal planes and the incident X-rays (the Bragg angle), and 2θ is the angle between the incident and diffracted X-rays (the diffraction angle). XRD data are usually plotted against 2θ, so in calculations use half of it as θ.

faq.q: How is an n = 2 reflection treated?
faq.a: 2d sinθ = 2λ is the same equation as a first-order reflection from planes with spacing d/2, so the second-order reflection from (100) planes is treated as a reflection from (200) planes. This way, everything can be calculated with n = 1.

faq.q: What happens if longer-wavelength X-rays are used?
faq.a: For the same spacing θ becomes larger, so peaks are spread farther apart and easier to separate, but the constraint sinθ ≤ 1 reduces the number of planes that can be measured. Radiation such as Cr Kα is used for applications such as residual stress measurement.

消滅則.desc: Rules by which diffraction from certain indices cancels out and disappears because of the arrangement of atoms. In BCC, only planes with h + k + l even diffract; in FCC, only planes whose h, k and l are all even or all odd.

シェラーの式.desc: The equation D = Kλ/(β cosθ) for estimating crystallite size from the broadening of XRD peaks, where β is the full width at half maximum in radians and K is about 0.9.

EDS(エネルギー分散型X線分光法).desc: A method of elemental analysis that measures the energies of characteristic X-rays excited by an electron beam with a semiconductor detector. It measures all elements simultaneously in a short time, but its resolution is lower than that of WDS.

XPS(X線光電子分光法).desc: An analytical method that determines the elements in the top few nanometers of a surface and their chemical bonding state (oxidation state and so on) from the binding energies of photoelectrons emitted by X-rays.

SIMS(二次イオン質量分析法).desc: A method that mass-analyzes secondary ions ejected while the specimen is sputtered by primary ions. It can measure depth profiles of trace elements such as dopants with ppm to ppb sensitivity.

ステンレス鋼.desc: An alloy steel containing roughly 11% Cr or more, made rust-resistant by a passive surface film. By microstructure it is divided into austenitic, ferritic, martensitic and other grades.

about.p: Stainless steel resists rusting because a passive film consisting mainly of Cr oxide, a few nanometers thick, forms on the surface and prevents the metal from dissolving. Above roughly 11% Cr the film forms stably, and more Cr gives better corrosion resistance. In environments containing oxygen the film spontaneously re-forms even when scratched, but in chloride-rich environments it is broken at weak points, causing pitting and crevice corrosion. For seawater environments, Mo-bearing grades such as SUS316 (AISI 316) are chosen. Note that stainless steel only resists rust; it does not stay rust-free in every environment.

The representative grade SUS304 (18%Cr-8%Ni, JIS; AISI 304) is austenitic, with an FCC structure even at room temperature because Ni stabilizes austenite; it has good ductility and weldability and is nearly nonmagnetic in the annealed condition. Grades such as SUS430 (AISI 430), with almost no Ni, are BCC ferritic, magnetic and relatively inexpensive. Grades such as SUS410 (AISI 410), with about 13% Cr and higher carbon, are martensitic and harden on quenching, so they are used for cutlery and blades. In addition, duplex grades, roughly half austenite and half ferrite, have excellent strength and resistance to stress corrosion cracking.

When austenitic stainless steel is heated to about 500–800 °C, Cr carbides precipitate at grain boundaries, depleting the surrounding Cr and weakening passivity. This is called sensitization and causes intergranular corrosion in weld heat-affected zones. Countermeasures include low-carbon SUS304L (AISI 304L) and grades in which carbon is tied up as Ti or Nb carbides. Austenitic grades are also susceptible to stress corrosion cracking in hot chloride environments, and countermeasures include removing residual stress or switching to a duplex grade.

faq.q: Can stainless steel be attracted to a magnet?
faq.a: Ferritic and martensitic grades are attracted to magnets. Even nonmagnetic austenitic SUS304 becomes attracted to a magnet when heavily cold worked, because part of it turns into strain-induced martensite.

faq.q: What is the difference between SUS304 and SUS316?
faq.a: SUS316 (AISI 316) contains about 2–3% Mo, making it more resistant to pitting and crevice corrosion by chloride ions. In seawater or salty environments, SUS316 and similar grades are chosen.

faq.q: Does stainless steel harden on quenching?
faq.a: Martensitic grades harden on quenching, but austenitic and ferritic grades do not transform on cooling and so do not harden by quenching. Austenitic grades are strengthened by cold working.

加工硬化.desc: The increase in the stress needed for deformation as plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which become entangled with each other. Strength rises but ductility falls. Also called strain hardening.

about.p: When a metal is plastically deformed, dislocations multiply and their density increases by several orders of magnitude; they attract and entangle one another through their stress fields and become harder to move. Further deformation therefore requires a larger stress. This is work hardening. It is why cold-rolled sheet and drawn wire are stronger than before working, and for pure metals that cannot be strengthened by heat treatment, 5000-series aluminum alloys, austenitic stainless steels and the like, work hardening is the main strengthening method. In exchange, ductility and toughness decrease.

For many metals, the relation between true stress and true strain in the plastic region can be approximated as σ = Kεⁿ, where n is called the strain-hardening exponent (work-hardening exponent) and K the strength coefficient. The larger n, the more readily the material strengthens as deformation proceeds and the less localized deformation spreads, so necking is delayed and uniform elongation is larger. Under constant volume, necking can be estimated to begin when the true strain equals n. Annealed FCC copper and austenitic stainless steels have large n and are well suited to forming such as deep drawing.

When a work-hardened metal is heated, recovery occurs first, as dislocations rearrange and internal stresses fall; at higher temperatures, recrystallization produces new grains, lowering the strength greatly and restoring ductility. Alternating cold working and annealing allows large deformations without cracking. In hot working, done above the recrystallization temperature, recovery and recrystallization proceed during working, so almost no work hardening remains and large deformations can be applied with small forces, though it is inferior to cold working in surface oxidation and dimensional accuracy.

faq.q: What is the difference between work hardening and precipitation hardening?
faq.a: Both strengthen by obstructing dislocation motion, but in work hardening the obstacles are the entanglements of dislocations multiplied by deformation, whereas in precipitation hardening they are fine precipitates formed by aging.

faq.q: How is the amount of working expressed?
faq.a: For drawing and rolling, it is generally expressed as the reduction in cross-sectional area (percent cold work). Note that it is calculated from the area, not the diameter.

faq.q: Can a work-hardened material be returned to its original softness?
faq.a: Annealing above the recrystallization temperature produces new strain-free grains, and strength and ductility return to roughly their condition before working.

固溶強化.desc: A strengthening method in which lattice strain created by solute atoms dissolved in the matrix obstructs dislocation motion and raises the strength of a metal. There are interstitial and substitutional types.

回復.desc: The process, preceding recrystallization when a cold-worked metal is heated, in which dislocations annihilate and rearrange and internal stresses and electrical resistivity decrease. Hardness changes little.

再結晶.desc: The phenomenon in which new strain-free grains nucleate and grow when a metal storing deformation strain is heated. Strength decreases and ductility is restored.

黄銅.desc: An alloy of copper with zinc. 70/30 brass, with about 30% Zn, is single-phase α and highly ductile, while 60/40 brass, with about 40% Zn, contains the β phase and is stronger.

チタン合金.desc: An alloy with a density about 60% that of steel, excellent specific strength and corrosion resistance. Depending on the proportions of the HCP α phase and BCC β phase, it is classified as α, α+β or β type.

柱状晶.desc: In the solidification of castings, elongated grains that grow inside the surface chill zone in the direction opposite to heat flow. Equiaxed grains form in the center.

標準電極電位.desc: The equilibrium potential of an electrode reaction, such as that between a metal and its ions, under standard conditions, relative to the standard hydrogen electrode at 0 V. The more negative it is, the more easily the metal is oxidized.

about.h: The reference and what the potential means
about.p: The standard electrode potential is the equilibrium potential of the electrode reaction Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ ⇄ M under standard conditions, such as 25 °C and unit ion activity, expressed relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇄ H₂) at 0 V. For example, Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V, Fe²⁺/Fe is −0.44 V and Zn²⁺/Zn is −0.76 V. Active metals with more negative values tend to give up electrons and become cations readily, while noble metals with more positive values tend to resist ionization. The emf of a cell combining two electrodes is the potential of the noble side minus that of the active side.

about.h: Relation to the likelihood of corrosion
about.p: For a metal to corrode, a cathodic reaction must be paired with its dissolution. In neutral water this is oxygen reduction and in acidic solutions hydrogen evolution; if the metal's potential is below the potential of those reactions, corrosion is thermodynamically possible. Gold and platinum hardly corrode because their potentials are very noble. Zinc and magnesium, on the other hand, with active potentials, are used as sacrificial anodes to protect steel. Which metal dissolves when dissimilar metals are in contact can also be judged from their relative potentials.

The standard electrode potential is determined by equilibrium thermodynamics and tells you nothing about the rate of corrosion. Aluminum, at −1.66 V, and titanium, at −1.63 V, are very active, yet they resist real environments well thanks to their dense surface oxide films. Also, real solutions differ from standard conditions in ion concentration and temperature, and the potential changes according to the Nernst equation. When evaluating combinations of dissimilar metals, it is therefore common to use the ranking of corrosion potentials measured in real environments such as seawater (the galvanic series).

faq.q: What do “active” and “noble” mean?
faq.a: Metals whose electrode potentials lie on the negative side are called active (base), and those on the positive side noble. The more active a metal, the more readily it ionizes, and when dissimilar metals are in contact, the more active one dissolves.

faq.q: Is the ionization tendency the same as the standard electrode potential?
faq.a: The order of ionization tendency (the activity series) roughly corresponds to arranging standard electrode potentials from low to high. You can think of the standard electrode potential as expressing it numerically.

faq.q: Why does aluminum resist corrosion even though its potential is active?
faq.a: A dense, stable oxide film forms on its surface and prevents further reaction. The standard electrode potential shows only a tendency and does not include differences in rate caused by films.

不動態.desc: A state in which a dense oxide film a few nanometers thick forms on a metal surface and dissolution of a metal that should thermodynamically dissolve almost stops.

about.p: Iron, chromium, nickel, titanium, aluminum and other metals can, under the right conditions, form dense oxide (or hydroxide) films a few nanometers thick on their surfaces, reducing the dissolution rate by several orders of magnitude. This state is passivity. Even for metals that are active in potential, the film separates the metal from the environment, so actual corrosion becomes very slight. In stainless steel a Cr-rich film plays this role, and in titanium a TiO₂ film. The film is thin and invisible, so the metallic luster is preserved.

about.h: Conditions that maintain or break it
about.p: In environments containing oxygen or oxidizers, the passive film re-forms spontaneously even when scratched. Iron, for example, becomes passive in concentrated nitric acid and hardly dissolves. On the other hand, in oxygen-poor crevices or reducing acids such as hydrochloric acid, the film re-forms with difficulty, and once broken, active dissolution proceeds. Chloride ions in particular break the film locally at weak points, so pitting and crevice corrosion are problems for stainless steel in seawater. For passive materials, localized corrosion requires more attention than uniform corrosion.

about.h: Passivity seen through potential and current
about.p: In a polarization curve, which measures the dissolution current while the metal's potential is raised step by step, the current first increases with potential, but above a certain potential (the passivation potential) it drops abruptly and stays small over a wide range of potential. This range is the passive region. Raising the potential further reveals the transpassive region, where the film breaks down and the current rises again, or, with chlorides present, the pitting potential. The higher the pitting potential, the more resistant the material is to pitting, and it is used as an index for selecting and evaluating grades. Even for the same material, the pitting potential falls as temperature and chloride concentration rise.

faq.q: How thick is the passive film?
faq.a: In stainless steel it is a very thin film of a few nanometers. It is different from the thick oxide scale that forms during high-temperature oxidation.

faq.q: What is passivation treatment?
faq.a: A treatment in which stainless steel is immersed in an oxidizing solution such as nitric acid to remove surface contamination and iron particles and to ensure that a dense passive film forms.

faq.q: Why does stainless steel sometimes rust in seawater?
faq.a: Chloride ions break the passive film locally, causing pitting and crevice corrosion. Grades with a stronger film, such as Mo-bearing SUS316 (AISI 316), are the countermeasure.

局部電池.desc: On the surface of a single metal, anodic and cathodic regions formed by inclusions, strain, oxygen concentration differences and the like, through which corrosion proceeds as in a battery.

ガルバニック腐食.desc: Accelerated corrosion of the more active metal, acting as the anode, when metals of different potential are in contact in an electrolyte. Also called dissimilar-metal corrosion.

孔食.desc: Localized corrosion in which chloride ions or similar species locally break down the passive film and small pits are dug deeper. It is a problem for stainless steels and aluminum.

応力腐食割れ.desc: Crack growth at stresses below the yield stress when a susceptible material under tensile stress is exposed to a specific corrosive environment.

犠牲陽極.desc: An anode of zinc, aluminum alloy, magnesium or another metal more active than the metal to be protected, connected electrically so that it dissolves first and protects the metal as the cathode.

ファラデーの法則.desc: The law that the amount of substance changed by an electrode reaction is proportional to the charge passed. The mass dissolved or deposited is m = ItM/(nF).

理論容量.desc: The maximum charge an electrode material can store, expressed per unit mass. It is calculated as Q = nF/(3.6M) mAh/g; for graphite it is 372 mAh/g.

about.p: When 1 mol of electrode material reacts and exchanges n mol of electrons, the charge passed is nF coulombs (F is the Faraday constant, 96485 C/mol). Dividing by the formula weight M gives the charge per unit mass, and converting with 1 mAh = 3.6 C gives Q = nF/(3.6M) mAh/g. For graphite, 1 mol of C₆ (72.06 g/mol) takes up one Li⁺, giving 372 mAh/g; for LiCoO₂, extracting all of the one Li gives about 274 mAh/g. The value changes depending on which mass is used in the denominator, so it is important to check which state's mass the capacity is quoted per.

Not all of the calculated theoretical capacity can necessarily be used. In layered LiCoO₂, extracting more than about half the Li destabilizes the crystal structure and degradation proceeds through oxygen release and phase transitions, so practical capacity has been limited to about 140–150 mAh/g, roughly half the theoretical value. Graphite and LiFePO₄, by contrast, can be used close to their theoretical values. On the first charge, an SEI film forms on the anode surface and some lithium is lost, so the capacity obtainable from the cell is slightly smaller still.

The energy stored in a battery is the product of capacity and voltage. The larger the potential difference between the positive and negative electrodes, the more energy is stored for the same capacity. LiFePO₄ has a theoretical capacity of about 170 mAh/g, but its average voltage of about 3.4 V is lower than that of layered oxides (about 3.7–3.8 V), so its energy per mass is smaller. In addition, the whole cell includes the mass of the electrolyte, separator, current collectors and casing, so the energy density of a cell is far smaller than the value calculated from the active materials.

faq.q: Is a material with a larger theoretical capacity always a better electrode material?
faq.a: Capacity alone does not decide it. Voltage, cycle life, volume change, safety and cost also matter. Silicon has about ten times the theoretical capacity of graphite, but its large volume change makes it difficult to use on its own.

faq.q: What is the difference between mAh/g and Wh/kg?
faq.a: mAh/g is the charge stored per unit mass, and Wh/kg the energy stored per unit mass. Multiplying charge by the average voltage gives energy, and the value of mAh/g × V is numerically the value in Wh/kg.

faq.q: Do the capacities of the positive and negative electrodes need to match?
faq.a: The capacity of the cell is set by the electrode with the smaller capacity. In real cells, the anode capacity is generally designed to be slightly larger than the cathode's so that lithium metal does not plate on the anode.

層状岩塩型構造.desc: A structure in which Li layers and transition-metal layers alternate within close-packed oxygen. LiCoO₂ and LiNiO₂-based cathodes take this structure, and Li⁺ moves two-dimensionally between the layers.

スピネル型構造.desc: A structure of composition AB₂O₄ in which cations occupy tetrahedral and octahedral sites in cubic close-packed oxygen. The cathode LiMn₂O₄ has three-dimensional Li⁺ pathways.

オリビン型構造.desc: The structure of the mineral olivine, taken by the cathode LiFePO₄. Strong covalent bonds in PO₄ make it thermally stable, but Li⁺ diffusion is one-dimensional and electronic conductivity is low.

固体電解質.desc: A material that conducts ions while remaining solid but conducts almost no electrons. Examples include sulfide and oxide electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries and stabilized zirconia for fuel cells.

固体高分子形燃料電池.desc: A fuel cell whose electrolyte is a polymer membrane with sulfonic acid groups that conducts protons when hydrated. Abbreviated PEFC (also PEMFC); it is humidified to keep the membrane from drying and operates at about 80 °C.

ショックレー・クワイサー限界.desc: The upper limit on the theoretical efficiency of a single-junction solar cell. Balancing the transmission of light below the band gap against thermalization losses, it reaches a maximum of about 33% at about 1.34 eV under terrestrial sunlight.

熱電性能指数.desc: The dimensionless value ZT = S²σT/κ that expresses the conversion performance of a thermoelectric material. It is larger the higher the Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity and the lower the thermal conductivity.

about.h: The quantities that make up ZT
about.p: S is the Seebeck coefficient, the voltage generated per kelvin of temperature difference; σ is the electrical conductivity, κ the thermal conductivity and T the absolute temperature. S²σ in the numerator is called the power factor and is a measure of how much electrical power can be extracted from the material. The smaller κ in the denominator, the easier it is to maintain the temperature difference between the hot and cold sides. The units in S²σT/κ cancel, so ZT is dimensionless. For example, a material with S = 200 µV/K, σ = 1.0×10⁵ S/m and κ = 1.5 W/(m·K) has ZT = 0.8 at 300 K.

The maximum efficiency of thermoelectric power generation is expressed as the Carnot efficiency, set by the hot- and cold-side temperatures, multiplied by a factor determined by ZT. The larger ZT, the closer the efficiency approaches the Carnot efficiency, but even at ZT = 1 the efficiency is only about 20% of the Carnot efficiency (about 17–24% depending on the temperatures). Bi₂Te₃-based materials near room temperature, PbTe- and Mg₂Si-based materials at intermediate temperatures, and SiGe, silicides and oxides at high temperatures are researched and used, so the materials with high ZT differ by operating temperature range.

about.h: Why ZT is hard to raise
about.p: S, σ and κ are not independent of one another. Raising the carrier concentration increases σ but lowers S, and the thermal conductivity carried by electrons also increases according to the Wiedemann–Franz law. The optimum carrier concentration therefore lies in the range of heavily doped semiconductors, about 10¹⁹–10²⁰ cm⁻³. Efforts are thus made to lower the lattice thermal conductivity by scattering only the phonons, which carry much of the heat, using nanostructured interfaces, point defects or atoms rattling inside cage-like crystals, while disturbing electron conduction as little as possible.

faq.q: Why are metals unsuitable as thermoelectric materials?
faq.a: Metals have high electrical conductivity, but their Seebeck coefficients are small, a few µV/K, and their electronic thermal conductivity is large, so ZT is extremely small. Heavily doped semiconductors are used as thermoelectric materials.

faq.q: Does ZT change with temperature?
faq.a: Yes. S, σ and κ all depend on temperature, and the ZT expression itself contains T. Each material has a temperature range where ZT is highest, so materials are chosen to match the operating temperature.

faq.q: Does ZT also matter for Peltier cooling?
faq.a: Yes. The coefficient of performance of thermoelectric cooling (Peltier devices) also increases with ZT, so ZT is the index of material performance for both power generation and cooling.

CFRP(炭素繊維強化プラスチック).desc: A composite of carbon fibers bound with epoxy or another resin. With low density and high modulus and strength, it excels in specific stiffness and is used in aircraft, automobiles and sporting goods.

about.p: CFRP is a composite of carbon fibers about 5–7 µm in diameter bound with a thermosetting resin such as epoxy or with a thermoplastic. Carbon fiber has a low density of about 1.8 g/cm³ and a Young's modulus of about 230 GPa for standard grades and several hundred GPa for high-modulus grades. In the fiber direction of unidirectional material, its specific stiffness (Young's modulus/density) is more than three times that of steel or aluminum alloys, and it also resists fatigue well, so it is used for the wings and fuselages of aircraft where weight must be saved, automobiles, wind turbine blades, fishing rods, golf clubs and more.

Unidirectional material is strong and stiff along the fibers, but perpendicular to the fibers and in in-plane shear it shows only low values close to those of the resin. Real parts are therefore made as laminates stacking plies of different orientations, such as 0°, ±45° and 90°, placing fibers to match the directions of load. When similar in-plane properties are wanted in every direction, a quasi-isotropic layup is used. The through-thickness direction is supported by the resin alone, so interlaminar strength is low and impact readily causes internal delamination, which requires attention.

Carbon fiber conducts electricity and has a noble electrode potential, so direct contact with aluminum alloys readily causes galvanic corrosion of the aluminum. At joints, a layer of glass fiber is interposed or titanium alloy fasteners are used. CFRP made with thermosetting resin cannot be melted after curing, so recycling is difficult, and technologies to recover the fibers by pyrolysis and other methods are being developed. Voids and fiber waviness from molding reduce strength, so parts are inspected by ultrasonic testing and similar methods.

faq.q: Is CFRP stronger than steel?
faq.a: In specific strength and specific stiffness, the tensile strength and Young's modulus in the fiber direction divided by density, it far exceeds steel. But its strength perpendicular to the fibers and through the thickness is low, so it is not stronger than steel in every direction.

faq.q: How are CFRP and GFRP chosen between?
faq.a: CFRP is generally used for parts where lightness and stiffness are critical and a high price is acceptable, and GFRP for parts where cost must be kept down or where electrical insulation or transparency to radio waves is required.

faq.q: Does CFRP rust?
faq.a: CFRP itself does not rust as metals do, but the resin can degrade from moisture absorption and ultraviolet light. It can also promote galvanic corrosion of metals it contacts, so joints with dissimilar materials need countermeasures.

GFRP(ガラス繊維強化プラスチック).desc: A composite of glass fibers bound with resin. It is less stiff than CFRP but inexpensive, electrically insulating and transparent to radio waves, and is used for boat hulls, bathtubs, printed circuit boards and more.

臨界繊維長.desc: The length needed for the stress at the middle of a short fiber to reach the fiber's tensile strength through interfacial shear. It is given by lc = σf·d/(2τc); fibers shorter than this pull out.

about.h: Why there is a critical length
about.p: Load is transferred to a short fiber in a matrix mainly through shear at the interface along the fiber's sides. At the fiber ends the stress is nearly zero; moving away from an end, load enters gradually through the interfacial shear stress τc and the fiber stress increases. The length at which load entering from both ends brings the stress at the fiber's middle exactly to its tensile strength σf is the critical fiber length lc, and force balance gives lc = σf·d/(2τc) (d is the fiber diameter). For carbon fiber in epoxy, lc is a few tenths of a millimeter to about 1 mm.

If a fiber is shorter than lc, its stress never reaches the tensile strength, and the fiber pulls out of the matrix before it breaks, so its strength cannot be fully exploited. If the fiber is much longer than lc, the low-stress end portions make up a small fraction, and reinforcement close to that of continuous fibers is obtained. As a rough guide, fibers more than about fifteen times lc are regarded as close to continuous. The stronger the interfacial adhesion, the larger τc and the shorter lc, and the thinner the fiber, the shorter lc.

In injection-molded short-fiber-reinforced plastics, fibers break and shorten during compounding and molding, and when the average fiber length approaches lc, the reinforcing effect drops sharply. Long-fiber pellets that keep fibers long and adjustments to molding conditions are therefore used. Pull-out also absorbs energy during fracture, so a certain amount of pull-out can help toughness. In ceramic matrix composites, the interface is made weak to deliberately induce pull-out, preventing sudden fracture and raising toughness.

faq.q: Does strengthening the interface shorten the critical fiber length?
faq.a: Yes. lc is inversely proportional to the interfacial shear strength τc, so strengthening adhesion with a coupling agent or similar shortens it, letting even short fibers use their strength.

faq.q: What changes if the fibers are made thinner?
faq.a: lc is proportional to the fiber diameter d, so thinner fibers have shorter critical lengths. For fibers of the same length, thinner ones have a larger ratio of length to lc, improving reinforcing efficiency.

faq.q: Can the critical fiber length be ignored for continuous fibers?
faq.a: Even with continuous fibers, when a single fiber breaks somewhere along its length, a length of about lc is needed on each side of the break for the stress to recover. This length also bears on how a fiber break affects neighboring fibers and on how strength scatter is treated.

疑似等方積層.desc: A laminate, such as [0/±45/90]ₛ, stacked from plies whose fiber directions are divided at equal angles. The in-plane Young's modulus is nearly equal in all directions, but the through-thickness direction remains weak.

層間はく離.desc: Damage in which the resin or interface between plies of a laminate cracks and the plies separate. It occurs because the through-thickness strength is low, and when caused internally by impact it is hard to detect from outside.

シランカップリング剤.desc: A compound with, in a single molecule, a group that bonds to inorganic materials and a group that reacts with resin. It is used to treat the surface of glass fibers, improving interfacial adhesion and water resistance.

金属基複合材料.desc: A composite (MMC) with a metal matrix such as aluminum reinforced by SiC particles or fibers. It can raise stiffness and wear resistance and lower thermal expansion.

セラミックス基複合材料.desc: A composite (CMC) with a ceramic matrix such as SiC reinforced by ceramic fibers. A weak interface lets fibers pull out, giving a material that does not fail suddenly.

比表面積.desc: The surface area per unit mass of a powder or porous body, in m²/g. For spherical particles S = 6/(ρd), increasing in inverse proportion to particle size.

BET法.desc: A method that physically adsorbs a gas such as nitrogen onto a powder at low temperature, fits the BET equation to the adsorption isotherm, and obtains the specific surface area from the monolayer capacity.

about.p: The BET method is based on a theory by Brunauer, Emmett and Teller that extends Langmuir's monolayer adsorption to handle multilayer adsorption. After the specimen is heated and degassed to remove surface moisture and the like, it is cooled to liquid-nitrogen temperature (about 77 K), and the amount adsorbed is measured while the relative pressure p/p₀ of nitrogen gas is varied. Fitting the resulting adsorption isotherm with the BET equation gives the monolayer capacity vm, the amount needed to cover the surface with exactly one layer. Converting vm to a number of molecules and multiplying by the area occupied by one nitrogen molecule, about 0.162 nm², gives the surface area.

about.h: The range over which the BET equation is fitted
about.p: The BET equation usually holds well over a relative pressure range of about 0.05–0.3. At lower pressures, surface heterogeneity, and at higher pressures, capillary condensation in pores, become significant, causing deviations from linearity. vm and the constant C are found from the slope and intercept of the straight line in the BET plot, and you also check, for example, that C is positive. For highly porous materials the value can change with the choice of fitting range, so it is important to record the measurement conditions when comparing. To measure small surface areas precisely, krypton is sometimes used instead of nitrogen.

about.h: Conversion to particle size and comparison with other methods
about.p: Assuming the particles are dense spheres of equal size, the particle size (BET diameter) can be estimated from the specific surface area S as d = 6/(ρS). The BET method counts all surface that gas molecules can reach, so even when primary particles are gathered with point contacts, nearly all their surface is measured. The BET diameter is therefore close to the primary particle size seen by TEM and usually comes out smaller than sizes from dynamic light scattering or laser diffraction, which measure whole agglomerates in liquid. Conversely, a BET diameter much smaller than the TEM size indicates open pores or roughness on the particle surfaces.

faq.q: Can the BET method measure the surfaces of closed pores?
faq.a: No. The inner surfaces of closed pores that gas molecules cannot enter from outside do not take part in adsorption, so they are not included in the BET specific surface area.

faq.q: How does the BET diameter differ from the crystallite size from the Scherrer equation?
faq.a: The BET diameter is a size derived from the surface area of the particles, while the Scherrer equation gives the size of coherent crystal domains (crystallites). When a single particle consists of several crystallites, the BET diameter is larger than the crystallite size.

faq.q: Why is the specimen heated and degassed before measurement?
faq.a: If moisture or gases adsorbed on the surface remain, the area available for nitrogen adsorption is reduced and the specific surface area is underestimated. The temperature is chosen within a range that does not alter the specimen.

ナノ粒子の融点降下.desc: The lowering of the melting point of nanoparticles below that of the bulk due to the surface energy contribution. The depression is roughly inversely proportional to particle size and becomes pronounced for particles a few nanometers across.

カーボンナノチューブ.desc: A carbon material formed by rolling graphene into a tube about 1 nm to several tens of nanometers in diameter. Depending on the rolling direction (the chiral indices) it can be metallic or semiconducting, and its strength along the axis is extremely high.

about.p: A carbon nanotube (CNT) has the structure of graphene, carbon atoms arranged in hexagons by sp² bonds, rolled seamlessly into a cylinder. There are single-walled CNTs with just one layer and multiwalled CNTs with many concentric layers; the interlayer spacing of multiwalled CNTs is about 0.34 nm, close to that of graphite. The rolling direction is given by the pair of integers (n, m) of the chiral vector Ch = na₁ + ma₂, which becomes the circumference; n = m is called armchair, m = 0 zigzag, and the rest chiral. The diameter can be calculated as d = a√(n² + nm + m²)/π (a = 0.246 nm), and most single-walled CNTs are about 1–2 nm.

The electronic states of a single-walled CNT are determined by which of graphene's band states survive, namely only the wave vectors allowed as standing waves around the circumference. When a line of allowed wave vectors passes through the K point, where graphene's conduction and valence bands touch, that is, when n − m is a multiple of 3, the tube is metallic; otherwise it is semiconducting. All armchair tubes are metallic. The band gap of semiconducting CNTs is roughly inversely proportional to the diameter, a few tenths of an eV to about 1 eV at a diameter of about 1 nm. Ordinary synthesis produces a mixture of metallic and semiconducting tubes, so separation or selective growth is a challenge for applications such as transistors.

about.h: Mechanical and thermal properties and uses
about.p: Along their axis, CNTs are joined only by strong sp² bonds, so they have a very high Young's modulus of about 1 TPa and tensile strengths of several tens of GPa, with a low density of about 1.3–2 g/cm³. Their axial thermal conductivity is also high. Exploiting these properties, they are used as small additions to resins and rubbers to raise conductivity and strength, as conductive additives in lithium-ion battery electrodes, in transparent conductive films and as interconnect materials. To bring out the outstanding properties of a single CNT in large materials such as bundles, yarns and composites, however, dispersion, alignment and load transfer between CNTs must be engineered.

faq.q: How are carbon nanotubes made?
faq.a: Besides arc discharge and laser ablation, mass production mainly uses chemical vapor deposition (CVD), in which hydrocarbons are decomposed and CNTs grow from fine catalyst particles of iron, cobalt and the like. The CNT diameter can be controlled to some extent by the size of the catalyst particles.

faq.q: If (n, m) are chosen at random, what fraction is metallic?
faq.a: n − m is a multiple of 3 about one third of the time, so about one third are metallic and about two thirds semiconducting.

faq.q: Can multiwalled carbon nanotubes be semiconducting too?
faq.a: Multiwalled CNTs contain a mixture of metallic and semiconducting layers, and the band gaps of the wide outer layers are small, so overall they usually show metallic conduction.
