グラフェン.desc: A single atomic layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb lattice by sp² bonds. Its band gap is essentially zero, its electron mobility is high, and its theoretical specific surface area counting both sides is about 2630 m²/g.

量子ドット.desc: A semiconductor nanocrystal a few nanometers across that confines electrons and holes in three dimensions. The confinement energy is roughly inversely proportional to the square of the size, so the emission wavelength can be tuned by size.

ボトムアップ法.desc: Methods of making nanomaterials by assembling atoms and molecules through nucleation and growth, such as liquid-phase reduction and thermal decomposition, the sol-gel method and CVD. The counterpart of top-down methods, which break down larger materials.

ゼータ電位.desc: The potential at the slipping plane outside the layer that moves with a particle in a liquid. The larger its absolute value, the stronger the electrostatic repulsion between particles and the more stable the dispersion. It is nearly zero at the isoelectric point.

材料選択図(アシュビーの図).desc: A chart that plots two properties, such as Young's modulus and density, on log–log axes and shows the range of each material family. Lines of constant performance index are straight, and the chart is used to compare candidates.

about.p: A materials selection chart plots two properties on the vertical and horizontal axes, such as Young's modulus versus density, strength versus density or fracture toughness versus strength, and shows the ranges of values for many materials. Because the values span many orders of magnitude, both axes are logarithmic. Members of the same material family cluster together; on the modulus–density chart, ceramics and metals occupy the upper right, polymers and woods the middle, and foams the lower left. Individual materials are shown as ellipses or bubbles covering the range of variation with composition and processing, and material families as larger envelopes around them.

Writing the condition for a constant performance index in logarithms gives a straight line. For example, E/ρ = C gives log E = log ρ + log C, a line of slope 1; √E/ρ = C gives a line of slope 2; and ∛E/ρ = C a line of slope 3. Materials on a line parallel to it perform equally in that application, and performance increases as the line is shifted toward the upper left. Drawing such a line on the chart and moving it step by step narrows the field to the materials remaining above the line as promising candidates. Because the slope changes with the loading mode, the winning materials on the same chart change with the application.

about.h: Its role in the selection procedure
about.p: In Ashby's method, the design requirements are first organized into function, constraints, objective and free variables, and candidates are screened by constraints such as service temperature and corrosion resistance. Next, the surviving candidates are ranked by the performance index derived from the objective, and finally the top candidates are researched for ease of fabrication into the actual shape, joining, price fluctuations, service history and so on before deciding. The selection chart is a tool for doing this screening and ranking visually. A major advantage of using it is that candidates can be surveyed across material families without fixing on a particular material from the start.

faq.q: Why are log–log axes used?
faq.a: Because Young's modulus spans many orders of magnitude, from about 0.001 GPa for foams to about 1000 GPa for diamond. Also, power-law performance indices appear as straight lines, which makes comparison simple.

faq.q: Can a material be chosen from the chart values alone?
faq.a: No. The chart is a tool for narrowing down candidates, and its values are typical ranges for material families. The final decision is made by researching data for specific alloys and grades, processing methods, cost and service history.

faq.q: Are there charts that use strength?
faq.a: Yes. On strength–density charts, guidelines for σf/ρ or ∛(σf²)/ρ are drawn, and on fracture toughness–strength charts, lines of K_IC/σy, to look for light, strong materials or materials resistant to fracture.

材料選択の性能指数.desc: The combination of material properties to be maximized in materials selection: E/ρ for a stiffness-limited tie, √E/ρ for a beam, ∛E/ρ for a plate, and σf/ρ for a strength-limited tie.

about.p: A performance index emerges when the free variables (such as section dimensions) are eliminated, using the constraints (specified stiffness or strength), from the equation expressing the objective (such as mass). For a tie of specified stiffness, the extension condition fixes the cross-sectional area as A ∝ 1/E, and the mass is m = ρAL ∝ ρ/E. So the larger E/ρ, the lighter the tie can be made. In this way, performance separates into the product of three parts, the functional requirements such as load and length, a factor for the shape of the cross section, and the material properties, and the material part alone is the performance index. Even after the shape and dimensions are optimized, the ranking of materials is determined by this index.

For a beam of square section whose dimensions can be varied freely, bending stiffness is proportional to the fourth power of the dimension, so mass is proportional to ρ/√E and the performance index is √E/ρ. For a plate of fixed width whose thickness alone can be varied, stiffness is proportional to the cube of the thickness, giving ∛E/ρ. When strength is the constraint, the indices become σf/ρ for a tie, ∛(σf²)/ρ for a beam and √σf/ρ for a plate. The deeper the root in the index, the relatively greater the influence of density, so low-density materials such as wood, magnesium alloys, CFRP and foams are favored for beams and plates in bending.

about.h: Extension to cost and environmental impact
about.p: When the objective is material cost instead of mass, density multiplied by the price per kg Cm, ρCm, is used, and for a stiffness-limited tie, E/(ρCm) is maximized. When the objective is the energy or CO₂ emissions of production, the per-kg value is multiplied in the same way. In thermal design, indices combining thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity are used. Note, however, that performance indices are derived on assumptions such as keeping the shape geometrically similar, so they may not be directly comparable when the cross-sectional shape differs greatly between materials or when there is a lower limit on dimensions.

faq.q: If the specific stiffness E/ρ is the same, is the performance as a beam also the same?
faq.a: No. The performance index for a beam is √E/ρ, so even with the same E/ρ, the lower-density material is better as a beam. Steel and aluminum alloys have almost the same E/ρ, but as beams the aluminum alloy is lighter.

faq.q: Does a performance index have units?
faq.a: Yes. For example, the unit of √E/ρ is something like √GPa/(Mg/m³). Indices with the same units can be compared in magnitude, but the value of an index itself has no particular physical meaning.

faq.q: What if there are two or more constraints?
faq.a: Calculate the required dimensions and mass for each constraint, and for each material compare using the larger mass (the more restrictive constraint). Which constraint is active varies from material to material.

比剛性.desc: Young's modulus divided by density, E/ρ, also called specific modulus. Steel, aluminum alloys and titanium alloys are all roughly the same, at about 25 GPa/(g/cm³).

破壊前降伏.desc: The condition in which, even with a crack present, the whole component yields first and sudden brittle fracture does not occur. The allowable crack size is proportional to (K_IC/σy)², so K_IC/σy serves as the performance index.

ライフサイクルアセスメント.desc: A method (LCA) for quantitatively evaluating energy consumption and environmental impact at each stage: material production, product manufacture, use, and disposal or recycling.

トランプエレメント.desc: Elements such as copper and tin that get mixed into steel scrap, are hard to remove by refining, and accumulate in steel with each recycling. They cause quality problems such as surface cracking during hot working.

パレート最適.desc: A state in which improving any one of several objectives necessarily worsens another. For competing objectives, candidates are chosen from the Pareto front using an exchange constant.

磁区.desc: A small region inside a ferromagnet or ferrimagnet in which the magnetization points in one direction. The material splits into many domains to lower the magnetostatic energy of its surface poles.

about.h: Why a material splits into domains
about.p: Inside a ferromagnet, the exchange interaction tends to align the magnetic moments of neighboring atoms parallel. If the whole crystal is magnetized in one direction, however, large magnetic poles appear on its surface, creating fields in the surrounding space and inside, with a large magnetostatic energy. Splitting into domains with different directions lets the poles cancel and lowers this energy greatly. Triangular closure domains can also form near the surface so that the flux closes on itself. This is why iron, though ferromagnetic, does not act as a magnet when no external field has been applied.

The boundary between domains is called a domain wall, and within it the magnetic moments turn gradually over a width of tens to hundreds of atoms. Turning abruptly raises the exchange energy, while turning slowly increases the number of moments tilted away from the easy axis and raises the anisotropy energy, so the wall thickness is set by the balance between the two and is proportional to √(A/K), where A is the exchange stiffness and K the anisotropy constant. A wall has an energy per unit area, so dividing into too many domains does not pay. The actual domain size is set by the balance between the decrease in magnetostatic energy and the increase in wall energy.

When a field is applied to a demagnetized ferromagnet, the domains oriented closest to the field first grow by domain-wall motion. As the field is increased further, the magnetization inside the domains rotates from the easy axis toward the field, approaching the saturation magnetization. Domain walls get caught at grain boundaries, precipitates and sites of internal stress, so how easily the walls move governs the coercivity and permeability. In soft magnetic materials, impurities and strain are reduced so the walls move easily; in permanent magnets, microstructures are created in which reversed domains are hard to nucleate or grow.

Domains can be observed by the Bitter method, in which a liquid of fine magnetic particles is applied to the surface and the particles gathering at the walls are viewed; by magneto-optical Kerr effect microscopy, which uses the rotation of polarized light; and by magnetic force microscopy (MFM), which detects the stray field from the surface with a magnetic tip. In electron microscopes, Lorentz microscopy and electron holography reveal the distribution of magnetization inside a specimen. In grain-oriented electrical steel, a technique is used in which fine grooves or strain are introduced on the surface by laser to refine the domains and lower the loss due to eddy currents.

faq.q: Are magnetic domains the same as grains?
faq.a: No. A grain is a region in which the atoms are arranged with the same orientation, and a domain is a region in which the magnetization points in the same direction. One grain can contain many domains, and a small particle can be a single domain as a whole (single-domain). Domain walls, the boundaries between domains, move under an applied field independently of grain boundaries.

faq.q: What happens to the domains when a magnet is heated?
faq.a: As the temperature rises the spontaneous magnetization decreases, and above the Curie temperature the spontaneous magnetization itself disappears and the material becomes paramagnetic, so the domains vanish as well. Cooling below the Curie temperature forms domains again, but without an external field they split into many domains with unaligned directions, so the magnet's magnetization does not return.

faq.q: What is a single-domain particle?
faq.a: In particles smaller than a certain size (the critical size), the energy needed to create a domain wall exceeds the reduction in magnetostatic energy, so the whole particle becomes a single domain. This is a single-domain particle. Reversing its magnetization requires rotating the whole magnetization, so the coercivity is large. Making it smaller still, however, leads to superparamagnetism, in which the magnetization reverses thermally.

磁壁.desc: The transition layer at the boundary between neighboring domains, across which the direction of the magnetic moments rotates gradually. Its thickness is set by the balance between exchange and anisotropy energies.

飽和磁化.desc: The magnetization when a strong field aligns all the magnetic moments in the same direction. For iron it is about 1.7×10⁶ A/m (about 2.2 T as µ₀Ms), and it decreases as the temperature rises.

フェリ磁性.desc: Magnetism in which the moments of two antiparallel sublattices differ in size, leaving a spontaneous magnetization equal to the difference. Ferrites such as magnetite are typical examples.

結晶磁気異方性.desc: The property that the ease of magnetization depends on the crystal direction. In iron, <100> is the easy axis. A large value raises coercivity, and a small one raises permeability.

超常磁性.desc: The state of very small ferromagnetic particles in which the barrier to reversal, KV, is small compared with the thermal energy, so the magnetization reverses thermally and the coercivity is almost zero.

最大エネルギー積.desc: The value (BH)max at which the magnitude of the product of flux density B and field H is greatest on the demagnetization curve of a permanent magnet. In kJ/m³, it measures a magnet's strength.

渦電流損失.desc: The loss due to Joule heating by eddy currents induced in a magnetic material when the flux changes under AC. It is proportional to the square of thickness and frequency and inversely proportional to resistivity.

引け巣.desc: A void in a casting where solidification shrinkage could not be made up by melt. It tends to form in thick sections that solidify last and is prevented by the design of risers and the order of solidification.

インベストメント鋳造.desc: A precision casting method in which a wax pattern is coated with refractory and hardened, and melt is poured into the mold left after the wax is melted out. Also called the lost-wax process; used for turbine blades and the like.

押出し.desc: Plastic working in which a billet in a container is pushed by a ram through a die opening to make long products of constant cross section. Aluminum profiles are a typical example.

スプリングバック.desc: The partial recovery of shape by elastic recovery when the load is removed after bending or other working. It is larger for materials with a higher yield stress and a lower Young's modulus.

溶接熱影響部.desc: The part of the base metal that did not melt during welding but whose microstructure and properties were changed by the welding heat. Also called the HAZ; hardening, softening, grain coarsening and sensitization can occur there.

about.p: A joint made by fusion welding such as arc welding is divided into the weld metal, which melted and solidified; the heat-affected zone (HAZ) outside it, which did not melt but received heat; and the base metal, which is hardly affected by heat. Within the HAZ, the peak temperature is higher closer to the boundary with the weld metal (the fusion line) and lower farther away. According to the peak temperature, the HAZ of steel is divided into bands such as a coarse-grained zone where grains have grown large, a fine-grained zone refined by transformation, an intercritical zone where only part transformed, and a tempered zone that does not transform, each with different hardness and toughness.

about.h: Hardening and cold cracking in the HAZ of steel
about.p: The part of the HAZ of steel heated into the austenite range is quenched as the surrounding cold base metal draws off its heat, so in steels of high hardenability it becomes hard martensite. When a hard microstructure, diffusible hydrogen from the weld metal and tensile stress from restraint coincide, cold cracking occurs some time after welding. The guide to hardenability is the carbon equivalent; in steels where it is high, preheating or postheating slows the cooling and lets hydrogen escape. Increasing the heat input also slows the cooling, but the grains in the coarse-grained zone can grow too large and the toughness can fall.

The problems that arise in the HAZ depend on the material. In austenitic stainless steels, Cr carbides precipitate at grain boundaries in the band exposed to about 500 to 800°C, causing sensitization and intergranular corrosion. In precipitation-hardened aluminum alloys and in materials strengthened by cold working, precipitates coarsen or the material recrystallizes, softening the HAZ so that the joint is weaker than the base metal. Even in high-strength steels strengthened by quenching and tempering, parts heated above the tempering temperature can soften. Joint design must allow for such strength loss in the HAZ.

faq.q: How wide is the heat-affected zone?
faq.a: It varies greatly with the welding process and heat input. In arc welding it is often a few mm, while in laser welding and electron beam welding, which have high energy density, the heat input is small and the zone is much narrower. The larger the heat input, and the thinner the plate so that heat escapes less easily, the wider the heat-affected zone.

faq.q: Can the properties of the heat-affected zone be restored after welding?
faq.a: To some extent. In steel, postweld heat treatment (stress-relief annealing) lowers residual stresses and tempers the hardened regions to restore toughness. Sensitization of stainless steel can be reversed by a solution heat treatment that dissolves the carbides again. In large structures, however, heat-treating the whole is difficult, so the basic approach is to prevent problems through the choice of material and welding conditions.

faq.q: Does friction stir welding also have a heat-affected zone?
faq.a: Yes. The material does not melt, but it is heated by friction, so outside the stir zone there form a thermo-mechanically affected zone, which received both heat and deformation, and a heat-affected zone, which received heat only. In precipitation-hardening aluminum alloys, precipitates coarsen and soften the material in this region, and it can be the weakest part of the joint.

炭素当量.desc: The sum of the effects of a steel's alloying elements on hardenability, converted into an amount of carbon. The higher the Ceq, the more the weld heat-affected zone hardens and the more likely cold cracking is.

鋭敏化.desc: The phenomenon in which stainless steel heated to about 500 to 800°C precipitates Cr carbides at grain boundaries, depleting the Cr around them and making the steel prone to intergranular corrosion.

熱間静水圧プレス.desc: A method that applies an equally high pressure from all directions with an inert gas at high temperature, to densify powder or eliminate closed internal pores in castings and sintered bodies. Abbreviated HIP.

ギブスエネルギー.desc: A state function defined by G = H − TS. At constant temperature and pressure, changes proceed spontaneously in the direction that lowers G, and the state of minimum G is equilibrium.

エリンガム図.desc: A diagram plotting the standard Gibbs energy change of formation of oxides and similar compounds, normalized per mol of O₂, against temperature. The lower its line, the more stable the oxide a metal forms.

about.h: How the diagram is drawn and the slope of the lines
about.p: An Ellingham diagram takes oxide formation reactions such as 2M + O₂ → 2MO, normalizes the standard Gibbs energy change ΔG° per mol of O₂, and plots it against temperature. Since ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and ΔH° and ΔS° hardly depend on temperature, each reaction gives a straight line whose slope is −ΔS°. In metal oxidation gaseous O₂ is taken into a solid and ΔS° is negative, so almost all lines slope upward, and oxides become less stable at higher temperature. At the temperatures where a metal or oxide melts or boils, ΔS° changes and the line bends.

At a given temperature, the lower the line, the more negative ΔG° is and the more stable the oxide. The vertical distance between 2 lines equals the ΔG° of the reaction in which the metal of the lower line reduces the oxide of the upper line, so metals near the bottom, such as Al, Mg and Ca, can reduce many oxides. The line for carbon, 2C + O₂ → 2CO, slopes downward because the number of gas molecules increases and ΔS° is positive, and at higher temperatures it lies below the lines of more and more metal oxides. This is why iron ore can be reduced with coke in a blast furnace. Above the temperature where a line crosses ΔG° = 0, the oxide decomposes even in 1 bar of oxygen.

about.h: The oxygen partial pressure scale and how to use it
about.p: At equilibrium ΔG° = RT ln pO₂, so joining a point on a line at a given temperature to the point ΔG° = 0 at 0 K and extending the line lets you read the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure. Many Ellingham diagrams carry an oxygen partial pressure scale for this purpose, and some also have scales for H₂/H₂O and CO/CO₂ ratios. They can be used to estimate the conditions that prevent steel from oxidizing in a heat-treatment atmosphere, whether an oxide decomposes in vacuum, and the conditions under which Cr is selectively oxidized in stainless steel. However, the diagram shows equilibria between pure substances; reaction rates and differences in activity within alloys must be considered separately.

faq.q: Does a metal lower in the Ellingham diagram always reduce the oxides above it?
faq.a: Thermodynamically it can, since the ΔG° of the reaction in that direction is negative, but whether it actually proceeds depends on the reaction rate, the removal of products and the activities. Reactions between solids proceed poorly if contact is poor, and they can stop when the oxide formed covers the surface. There are also examples, such as the thermite reaction, that proceed all at once with a large release of heat.

faq.q: Why is the Ellingham diagram drawn per mol of O₂?
faq.a: Because when the amount of oxygen is the same, taking the difference between 2 formation reactions cancels the O₂, and the vertical distance between the lines is directly the ΔG° of the redox reaction. If it were drawn per mol of oxide, the number of oxygen atoms would differ with the formula, and the lines could not be compared directly. Diagrams for sulfides and nitrides are drawn per mol of S₂ or N₂ on the same idea.

faq.q: Can the rate of oxidation be read from an Ellingham diagram?
faq.a: No. An Ellingham diagram shows the equilibrium ΔG° and only indicates the thermodynamic tendency for an oxide to form. Aluminum corrodes little even though its ΔG° is strongly negative, because a dense oxide film blocks diffusion; the rate is set by kinetics such as diffusion through the film.

平衡酸素分圧.desc: The oxygen partial pressure at which a metal and its oxide coexist in equilibrium. It is found from ΔG° = RT ln pO₂; above it the metal is oxidized, and below it the oxide is reduced.

活量.desc: The thermodynamic effective concentration of a component in a solution or solid solution, satisfying μ = μ° + RT ln a. It is 1 for the pure substance and equals the mole fraction in an ideal solution.

about.p: When the chemical potential of component i in a solution is written μi = μi° + RT ln ai, ai is the activity. μi° is the chemical potential in the reference state; in materials science the pure solid or liquid at the same temperature is often taken as the reference (ai = 1), and for gases the partial pressure divided by the standard pressure corresponds to the activity. In an ideal solution ai = xi (the mole fraction) by Raoult's law, and for real solutions one writes ai = γi·xi, with the activity coefficient γi expressing the deviation from ideality. Equilibrium constant expressions contain activities in place of concentrations.

When unlike atoms attract each other more weakly than like atoms, the component escapes from the solution more easily, giving γ > 1 (positive deviation from Raoult's law), and in extreme cases the solution separates into 2 phases. Conversely, when unlike atoms attract strongly, γ < 1 (negative deviation), indicating a tendency toward ordering or compound formation. In the regular solution model, it can be written RT ln γA = Ω(1 − xA)² using the interaction parameter Ω. In the dilute range of a solute, γ becomes nearly constant, and Henry's law, in which activity is proportional to concentration, holds.

The equilibrium of metal oxidation 2M + O₂ → 2MO is expressed by ΔG° = −RT ln K with K = a(MO)² ÷ (a(M)² × pO₂). If the activity of metal M in an alloy is less than 1, the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure is higher for the same ΔG°, and M becomes harder to oxidize. Conversely, if the oxide formed dissolves in another oxide and its activity falls, oxidation proceeds more easily. Removing impurity oxides by dissolving them into slag in smelting, and finding the amount of hydrogen or nitrogen dissolved in a molten metal from the gas partial pressure (Sieverts' law), are also based on equilibrium thinking with activities.

faq.q: How is activity different from concentration?
faq.a: Concentration expresses how much of a component is present, while activity expresses how strongly that component acts in chemical reactions and phase equilibria. In an ideal solution the mole fraction and activity coincide, but in real solutions with atomic interactions they differ by the activity coefficient. It is activity that is used in the expressions for equilibrium constants and chemical potentials.

faq.q: Why is the activity of a pure solid 1?
faq.a: Because the pure solid itself is chosen as the reference state. If the chemical potential of the reference state is μ°, then for the pure substance μ = μ°, so ln a = 0, that is, a = 1. Choosing another reference changes the value, but in equilibrium calculations ΔG° is put on the same reference, so the result does not change.

faq.q: Can activity exceed 1?
faq.a: With the pure substance as the reference, it does not exceed 1 in a solution in stable equilibrium. If it did, the free energy would be lowered by precipitating that component as the pure substance. In supersaturated states, or with another reference based on Henry's law (such as a dilute 1 wt% solution), values above 1 can occur.

化学ポテンシャル.desc: The rate at which the Gibbs energy of a system increases when 1 mol of a component is added (the partial molar Gibbs energy). In phase equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is equal in all phases.

正則溶液.desc: A solution model in which the entropy of mixing is the same as for an ideal solution and the enthalpy of mixing is Ωx(1 − x). When Ω is positive, a miscibility gap appears at low temperature.

混合エントロピー.desc: The entropy that arises because mixing increases the number of ways atoms can be arranged. In an ideal solution it is −R[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)], with its maximum at x = 0.5.

スピノーダル分解.desc: Phase separation into 2 phases at compositions where the free energy curve is convex upward, in which composition fluctuations grow without a nucleation barrier. Uphill diffusion produces a periodic structure.

生体適合性.desc: The ability of a material to perform the required function in a specific application with an appropriate host response. It is evaluated including not only the material but also its shape, surface condition and location of use.

about.p: Biocompatibility is defined as "the ability of a material to perform with an appropriate host response in a specific application". In the past the emphasis was on not reacting and doing no harm in the body, but as materials that exploit active responses of the body increased, such as ceramics that bond to bone and polymers that are resorbed and replaced by tissue, it came to be judged by whether the desired response occurs for the application. Even the same material faces different requirements inside bone, in contact with blood and on the skin, so biocompatibility is an evaluation of a combination of material and application.

about.h: Host responses and the classification of materials
about.p: When a material is placed in the body, proteins first adsorb on its surface, and cells respond on top of them. Around bioinert materials a thin fibrous membrane often forms, separating the material from the surrounding tissue. Bioactive materials bond chemically to bone at their surface, and bioresorbable materials gradually degrade and are replaced by tissue. For materials in contact with blood, hemocompatibility, which suppresses platelet adhesion and thrombus formation, is important. Released ions and wear debris can cause inflammation or allergy, so not only the surface but also what is produced by degradation is evaluated.

Biocompatibility is evaluated by combining cytotoxicity tests, in which cells are exposed to the material or its extract, tests for sensitizing (allergic) and irritant reactions, genotoxicity tests, implantation tests in animals and others, and the framework is set out in the international standard for the biological evaluation of medical devices (the ISO 10993 series). Which tests are needed depends on the part of the body contacted and the duration. For implants, mechanical compatibility also matters: too little strength leads to failure, and too much stiffness relative to bone thins the bone by stress shielding. Only when both chemical safety and mechanical properties are in place is biocompatibility achieved for that application.

faq.q: Is a biocompatible material safe wherever it is used?
faq.a: No. Biocompatibility is an evaluation for each application, so a material that works without problems in bone may form thrombi where it contacts blood. The shape, surface condition, duration of use, wear debris and ion release also affect the outcome, so it must be confirmed for each application.

faq.q: Is a material more biocompatible the less it reacts in the body?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Some applications, such as the femoral heads of artificial joints, are best served by no reaction, but bioactive materials that bond to bone work well as bone defect fillers, and materials that are resorbed and disappear work well as sutures. Biocompatibility requires that the response needed in that application occurs.

faq.q: Why is titanium used so widely as a biomaterial?
faq.a: Because the TiO₂ passive film on its surface is stable in body fluids and gives high corrosion resistance, and because osseointegration, in which bone contacts the surface directly, occurs. Its high specific strength and its lower Young's modulus than stainless steel or Co-Cr alloys are also advantages.

応力遮蔽.desc: A phenomenon in which an implant far stiffer than bone carries most of the load, the mechanical stimulus to the surrounding bone falls, and the bone is resorbed and thins.

about.p: When bone and an implant are joined and carry a load together, both strain by nearly the same amount, so the stress is shared in proportion to Young's modulus. The Young's modulus of cortical bone is about 10–30 GPa, whereas stainless steel is about 200 GPa, Co-Cr alloys about 210 GPa and Ti-6Al-4V about 110 GPa. When a high-modulus metal carries most of the load, the stress on the surrounding bone becomes smaller than it should be. From the bone's point of view the load is shielded, so the phenomenon is called stress shielding. It is a problem with the stems of artificial hip joints and with plates that fix fractures.

Bone changes the balance of formation and resorption according to the mechanical stimulus it receives, becoming thicker where it is used heavily and thinner where it is not (Wolff's law). Where stress shielding reduces the stimulus, resorption outpaces formation, bone density falls and the bone thins. As a result, loosening develops between implant and bone, or the bone becomes prone to fracture after the implant is removed. The weakening of bone during long bed rest or in weightlessness has the same mechanism. In artificial hip joints, bone loss is often said to be most noticeable near the upper end of the femur.

The basic remedy is to bring the stiffness of the implant closer to that of bone. On the materials side, β titanium alloys with a Young's modulus of about 55–80 GPa and porous metals whose modulus is lowered by pores have been developed. The Young's modulus of a porous body with open pores falls roughly with the square of the relative density, and bone growing into the pores also strengthens fixation. On the shape side, stems are made thinner and shorter, or designed to transfer load at a position close to the bone. However, lowering the stiffness too far risks implant deformation and fatigue failure, so it is decided in balance with strength.

faq.q: If the aim is a lower Young's modulus, why not make implants from polymers?
faq.a: Polymers often have a Young's modulus too far below that of bone, or cannot withstand the load in terms of strength, creep and fatigue, so on their own they are unsuitable for sites that carry large loads. Composites whose modulus is brought close to that of bone, such as carbon-fiber-reinforced PEEK, are used in spinal fixation devices and similar applications.

faq.q: Is stress shielding a change that makes bone stronger?
faq.a: No, the opposite. The implant takes over the load, so the stimulus to the bone falls, and the bone is resorbed and weakens. It is the opposite problem to bone failing under excessive stress.

faq.q: How is stress shielding investigated?
faq.a: Clinically, changes in bone mass around the implant are followed with X-ray images and bone density measurements. At the design stage, the stress distribution in bone and implant is calculated by the finite element method, and the drop in bone stress compared with the case without an implant is evaluated.

ハイドロキシアパタイト.desc: A calcium phosphate with the formula Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂. Close to the mineral component of bones and teeth, it is used as a bioactive ceramic that bonds directly to bone. Its Ca/P ratio is 1.67.

オッセオインテグレーション.desc: A state in which living bone and the implant surface are in direct contact without intervening fibrous tissue and can transfer load. It was discovered with titanium dental implants.

β型チタン合金.desc: A titanium alloy containing large amounts of β-stabilizing elements such as Nb, Ta and Mo, so that it has the BCC β phase even at room temperature. Its low Young's modulus reduces stress shielding in medical use.

超弾性.desc: The property, above the reverse transformation finish temperature, of recovering large strains of several percent on unloading through stress-induced martensitic transformation and its reverse. Ni-Ti alloys are the typical example.

生分解性高分子.desc: A polymer broken down in the body or the environment by hydrolysis or the action of microorganisms. Polylactic acid and polyglycolic acid are used in absorbable sutures and bone fixation devices.

骨セメント.desc: A material made by mixing PMMA powder with liquid methyl methacrylate and polymerizing it in the body to fix artificial joints to bone. It fixes them not by adhesion but by filling the gap and interlocking mechanically.

応力拡大係数.desc: A quantity expressing the strength of the stress field at a crack tip. Given by K = Yσ√(πa), it depends on both the stress and the crack length, and the crack grows unstably when it reaches a critical value.

about.h: The stress field at a crack tip
about.p: Near the tip of a crack in an elastic body, the stress grows in inverse proportion to the square root of the distance r from the tip, taking the form σ ∝ K/√(2πr). The shape of this distribution is the same regardless of the shape of the crack or the part, and only its strength is set by the stress intensity factor K. So even for a part and a test specimen of different shapes, the crack tips can be regarded as being in the same state if K is the same. This is why fracture toughness measured on small specimens can be used to design real structures. In reality the region near the tip yields and becomes a plastic zone, so this idea holds when the plastic zone is small enough.

about.h: The geometry factor Y and superposition
about.p: The stress intensity factor can be written K = Yσ√(πa), where the geometry factor Y depends on the shape and position of the crack, the width of the part and how the load is applied. For a central crack (length 2a) in an infinitely wide plate, Y = 1; for a short crack entering from the edge of a plate (an edge crack) it is about 1.12, and Y rises as the crack becomes large compared with the width of the part. Y for many geometries is compiled in handbooks as formulas and tables. Within the elastic range, when several loads such as tension and bending act together, K values of the same mode can be added, and the K from residual stress is also included in the assessment.

about.h: Relation to the energy release rate
about.p: The elastic energy released when a crack advances by a unit area is called the energy release rate G, related to K by G = K²/E in plane stress and G = K²(1 − ν²)/E in plane strain. Griffith's condition, that G equals the energy needed to create surfaces, is equivalent when written with K to K reaching a critical value K_c. The critical value for Mode I is the fracture toughness K_IC, and under repeated loading the range of K, ΔK, determines the fatigue crack growth rate. In this way, K is the quantity that links the assessment of both static fracture and fatigue.

faq.q: How does the stress intensity factor differ from the stress concentration factor?
faq.a: The stress concentration factor Kt is a dimensionless number giving how many times the average stress the maximum stress at a rounded hole or notch root is. When the tip is sharp, as at a crack, the maximum stress is in theory infinite and cannot be expressed by Kt, so the strength of the stress field at the tip is expressed by the stress intensity factor K (in MPa·√m).

faq.q: What do the units MPa·√m mean?
faq.a: In K = Yσ√(πa), σ is the stress (MPa) and a is the crack length (m), and since its square root is multiplied in, the units become MPa·√m. Even at the same stress, a crack 4 times longer doubles K. The square root of a length appears in the units because the effect of crack size is included.

faq.q: When can the stress intensity factor not be used?
faq.a: When the plastic zone at the crack tip is large compared with the crack length, the plate thickness or the remaining cross-section. In highly ductile materials, thin plates or under high loads, the plastic zone spreads and K alone cannot describe the state. In that case, elastic-plastic fracture mechanics quantities that include plasticity, such as the J-integral or the crack tip opening displacement (CTOD), are used.

グリフィスの理論.desc: The theory that fracture proceeds when the elastic energy released as a crack extends exceeds the energy of the new surfaces. The fracture stress is given by √(2Eγs/(πa)).

エネルギー解放率.desc: The elastic energy released when a crack advances by a unit area. Written G, it equals K²/E in plane stress, and the crack advances when it reaches the critical value G_c.

応力集中係数.desc: The number Kt giving how many times the average stress the maximum stress at a hole or notch root is. For an elliptical hole it is 1 + 2√(a/ρ), and for a circular hole it is 3.

パリス則.desc: The empirical law da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ, stating that the fatigue crack growth rate is proportional to a power of the stress intensity factor range. It is used to estimate crack growth life.

about.h: The three regions of the crack growth curve
about.p: Plotting the fatigue crack growth rate da/dN against the stress intensity factor range ΔK = K_max − K_min on log-log axes gives an S-shaped curve. In the region of small ΔK, the rate drops sharply as ΔK approaches the threshold ΔK_th, and below it the crack effectively does not grow. In the intermediate region the curve is a straight line, and expressing it as da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ is the Paris law. In the region where ΔK is large and the maximum stress intensity factor approaches the fracture toughness, the rate rises sharply and finally leads to unstable fracture. The region used to estimate life in design is mainly the intermediate one.

about.h: The exponent m and the constant C
about.p: The exponent m is roughly 2–4 for metals and can exceed 10 for ceramics. The larger m is, the more the growth rate changes with a small increase in stress or crack length. The value of the constant C changes with the unit system, so the data are used with consistent units, such as da/dN in m/cycle and ΔK in MPa·√m. It is also known that, among steels, differences in the intermediate-region rate due to microstructure and strength are relatively small. On the other hand, the rate is affected by mean stress (the stress ratio R), environment and temperature, so it is important to choose data measured under the conditions of use.

Substituting ΔK = YΔσ√(πa) into the Paris law and integrating from the initial crack length a₀ to the critical crack length a_f gives the number of cycles needed for the crack to grow. The critical length is set by the condition K_max = K_IC. Because growth is slow while the crack is short, most of the life is spent early on, and the result depends strongly on the estimate of a₀. In damage-tolerant design for aircraft and similar structures, a crack of a size that nondestructive inspection could miss is assumed to exist, and the inspection interval is set so that it is found at the next inspection before it reaches the critical size.

faq.q: Is the Paris law derived from theory?
faq.a: No, it is an empirical law obtained by organizing a large body of experimental data. There are models that try to explain the exponent from plastic deformation and blunting at the crack tip, but C and m are usually determined by tests on each material. Note also that it holds only in the intermediate region.

faq.q: If ΔK is below ΔK_th, will a crack never grow?
faq.a: Under constant-amplitude loading it is a guide below which the crack can be regarded as effectively not growing. However, when the crack is very short, when occasional large loads are mixed in, or in corrosive environments, cracks can grow even below ΔK_th.

faq.q: How does crack growth change when the stress ratio R changes?
faq.a: Even at the same ΔK, the larger R = σmin/σmax is (the higher the mean stress), the faster the growth rate tends to be and the smaller ΔK_th becomes. One main reason is crack closure: when the crack faces touch partway through unloading, the ΔK actually acting at the tip becomes smaller, but this effect weakens as R increases.

マイナー則.desc: The rule that adds up damage at different stress amplitudes as the sum of the ratios n/N of applied cycles to life, and regards fatigue failure as occurring when the sum reaches 1.

ストライエーション.desc: Fine lines seen on a fracture surface where a fatigue crack has advanced. Their spacing corresponds roughly to the crack growth per cycle, and they are observed with an electron microscope.

修正グッドマン線図.desc: A diagram expressing the effect of mean stress. It joins the fully reversed fatigue limit and the tensile strength with a straight line, taking σa = σw(1 − σm/σB) as a guide to the allowable stress amplitude.

フォノン.desc: A particle-like quantum of the lattice vibrations of a crystal. Phonons carry heat and heat capacity in insulators and also cause the scattering of electrons.

about.p: The atoms in a crystal are bound to one another as if joined by springs, and their vibrations can be expressed as a superposition of waves spread through the whole crystal. The energy of each wave is quantized in units of ħω, and a unit of this excitation is called a phonon, just as a photon is the quantum of an electromagnetic wave. There are acoustic phonons, in which neighboring atoms move in the same direction, and optical phonons, in which atoms within the unit cell move in opposite directions. The Debye temperature is a rough measure of the energy of the highest-frequency phonon converted to a temperature, and it is higher for stronger bonds and lighter atoms.

At high temperatures all vibrations are excited, each atom holds an energy of 3kT, and the molar heat capacity is about 3R (the Dulong–Petit law). As the temperature falls, phonons stop being excited in order from the highest energy, and the heat capacity shrinks. At temperatures well below the Debye temperature, only long-wavelength acoustic phonons are excited, and the heat capacity is proportional to T³. This quantum behavior of the heat capacity, which classical theory could not explain, was the starting point when Einstein and Debye explained the heat capacity of solids.

In insulators and semiconductors heat is carried mainly by phonons, and the thermal conductivity is expressed through the heat capacity, the speed of sound and the mean free path, as in κ = (1/3)Cvl. Phonons are scattered by other phonons, point defects and isotopes, dislocations, and grain boundaries and surfaces. At high temperatures umklapp processes between phonons dominate and κ falls roughly as 1/T, while at very low temperatures scattering at surfaces and grain boundaries dominates. Thermoelectric materials deliberately scatter phonons with nanostructures and heavy atoms to lower thermal conductivity, whereas heat-dissipating materials use crystals with little scattering instead.

faq.q: Is a phonon a real particle?
faq.a: It is a quantum of the collective vibration of atoms, not a particle that can be taken out on its own, and it is called a quasiparticle. Even so, it carries energy and crystal momentum and collides with and scatters electrons and photons, so treating it as a particle explains many phenomena simply.

faq.q: Do phonons carry heat in metals too?
faq.a: They do, but in pure metals the heat carried by conduction electrons is far larger, and the phonon share is usually only part of the total. In alloys and in intermetallic compounds with few electrons, the phonon share can become large.

faq.q: How are phonons related to electrical resistance?
faq.a: The main cause of the temperature dependence of the electrical resistance of metals is the scattering of conduction electrons by phonons. As temperature rises, phonons increase and so does scattering, and near room temperature the resistivity increases nearly in proportion to temperature. The fall in semiconductor mobility with temperature has the same cause.

デュロン・プティの法則.desc: The law that the molar heat capacity of many solid elements near room temperature is about 3R (about 25 J/(mol·K)). It corresponds to the classical limit of lattice vibrations at high temperature.

デバイ温度.desc: The highest frequency of lattice vibration converted, via its energy, to a temperature. Well below it, the lattice heat capacity is proportional to T³, and at high temperatures it approaches about 3R.

熱拡散率.desc: The quantity α = κ/(ρc), the thermal conductivity divided by the heat capacity per unit volume. It expresses how quickly a change in temperature spreads through a material and has units of m²/s.

about.h: How it differs from thermal conductivity
about.p: Thermal conductivity κ expresses how much heat flows under a temperature gradient, that is, how easily heat flows in a steady state. Thermal diffusivity α = κ/(ρc), by contrast, is the ratio of conducting heat easily to being hard to warm up (the heat capacity per unit volume ρc), and it expresses how quickly a change in temperature spreads. The transient heat conduction equation is ∂T/∂t = α∇²T, so the change of temperature with time is set by α, not by κ alone. A rough time for the temperature to change through a plate of thickness L is L²/α, which can be used to estimate heating and cooling times.

Near room temperature, the thermal diffusivity is about 1.1×10⁻⁴ m²/s for copper, about 1×10⁻⁴ m²/s for aluminum, about 1×10⁻⁵ m²/s for carbon steel, about 4×10⁻⁶ m²/s for stainless steel, about 5×10⁻⁷ m²/s for glass, and about 1×10⁻⁷ m²/s for wood and polymers. Diamond exceeds 10⁻³ m²/s. The heat capacity per unit volume differs only by a few times among solids, so thermal diffusivities rank broadly in the same order as thermal conductivities. Gases have low thermal conductivity but also low density, so their thermal diffusivity is larger than that of solid polymers.

Thermal diffusivity is commonly measured by the laser flash method. A pulse of light is applied to the front of a disk sample, and α is found as α = 0.1388L²/t½ from the time t½ for the temperature rise of the back face to reach half its maximum. Because the sample can be small and measurements can be made up to high temperatures, the thermal conductivity is often obtained by multiplying the measured α by the density and specific heat, as κ = αρc. Thermal diffusivity matters in heat problems that involve time, such as the spread of temperature in welding and heat treatment, the temperature difference between surface and interior on quenching, and estimates of transient heating in semiconductor devices.

faq.q: Does a material with a large thermal conductivity always have a large thermal diffusivity?
faq.a: Among solids this is often so, but materials with a large heat capacity per unit volume ρc have a small thermal diffusivity for their thermal conductivity. Choose the quantity according to whether the aim is to compare steady heat flow or the speed of temperature change.

faq.q: How does thermal diffusivity differ from thermal effusivity?
faq.a: Thermal diffusivity κ/(ρc) expresses how quickly a change in temperature spreads through a material, while thermal effusivity √(κρc) expresses how much heat a surface absorbs when heat is applied to it. The coldness felt on touching and the momentary temperature rise of a surface depend on the effusivity.

faq.q: Why does thermal diffusivity have the same units, m²/s, as a diffusion coefficient?
faq.a: Because the transient heat conduction equation ∂T/∂t = α∇²T has the same form as Fick's second law for the diffusion of matter, ∂C/∂t = D∇²C. The spread of temperature can be treated like the diffusion of atoms, with a characteristic distance of √(αt).

ヴィーデマン・フランツの法則.desc: The law that the ratio of a metal's thermal conductivity κ to its electrical conductivity σ is proportional to absolute temperature, κ = LσT, where L is the Lorenz number, about 2.44×10⁻⁸ W·Ω/K².

ウムクラップ過程.desc: Phonon-phonon scattering in which the total momentum changes by a reciprocal lattice vector. It counteracts heat flow and is the main reason the thermal conductivity of insulators falls at high temperatures.

線膨張係数.desc: The fractional change in length when the temperature rises by 1 K. It arises from the anharmonicity of the interatomic potential and tends to be smaller in strongly bonded materials with high melting points.

インバー.desc: An Fe-36%Ni alloy. Its magnetovolume effect cancels ordinary thermal expansion, giving a very small linear expansion coefficient of about 1×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ near room temperature.

真実接触面積.desc: The area where asperities on two surfaces actually touch. When the asperities deform plastically it equals the load divided by the hardness, and it is far smaller than the apparent contact area.

アーチャードの摩耗式.desc: The equation V = KWL/H, stating that wear volume V is proportional to the normal load W and sliding distance L and inversely proportional to hardness H. K is the wear coefficient, which varies widely with the wear mechanism.

about.p: Archard assumed that the real contact spots between two sliding surfaces produce wear debris with a certain probability during sliding. The real area of contact equals the load W divided by the hardness H, so the number of contact spots is proportional to W/H. The distance slid before a contact spot is replaced is about the size of the spot, so the number of opportunities to form wear debris over a sliding distance L is proportional to L. Putting these together, the wear volume can be written V = KWL/H. The dimensionless wear coefficient K has the meaning of the probability that a contact spot becomes wear debris.

about.h: Wear coefficient and specific wear rate
about.p: K is large, about 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻², for unlubricated adhesive wear between metals of the same kind, and falls to about 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁵ for mild wear protected by oxide films and to about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ under good lubrication. In practice, the specific wear rate k = V/(WL), which lumps K/H together without separating out the hardness, is often used, expressed in mm³/(N·m). Because the specific wear rate can also be used for polymers, composites and coatings, whose hardness is hard to define, it is widely used to compare wear resistance. When comparing values, it is important to match the test method and conditions.

The Archard equation is useful for life estimates and material comparisons in the mild-wear regime, where wear is proportional to load and sliding distance. However, above certain loads or speeds, frictional heat can break down oxide films or adhesion can spread, causing a transition to severe wear, with wear larger by orders of magnitude. The wear rate also changes during the initial running-in period. K should therefore be determined in tests close to the actual operating conditions, and the equation should be used after confirming where the wear regime changes.

faq.q: Why do harder materials wear less?
faq.a: In a harder material, the real area of contact needed to support the same load is smaller, so there are fewer contact spots producing wear debris. In abrasive wear too, a surface harder than sand grains and the like is hard to cut. Hard but brittle materials, however, can wear by cracking.

faq.q: Does enlarging the apparent contact area reduce wear?
faq.a: In the Archard equation, the wear volume does not depend on the apparent area. Enlarging the area lowers the pressure and temperature, however, making it easier to stay in the mild-wear regime, so in practice life can be extended. For the same volume, a larger area also means a shallower wear depth.

faq.q: How is the wear coefficient measured?
faq.a: In a pin-on-disk or ball-on-disk test, the specimen is slid under a set load and sliding distance, and the wear volume is found from the mass loss or the shape of the wear track. Dividing that volume by the load and sliding distance gives the specific wear rate, and multiplying by the hardness gives the dimensionless wear coefficient.

ストライベック曲線.desc: A curve plotting the friction coefficient of a plain bearing or similar contact against the bearing characteristic number, viscosity × speed ÷ pressure. It shows the transitions among boundary, mixed and hydrodynamic lubrication.

about.h: Shape of the curve and its three regions
about.p: The Stribeck curve plots the bearing characteristic number ηN/P (η is the lubricant viscosity, N the rotational speed and P the bearing pressure) on the horizontal axis against the friction coefficient on the vertical axis. The region of small ηN/P is boundary lubrication, where asperities on the surfaces touch and the friction coefficient is about 0.1. As ηN/P increases, the bearing enters mixed lubrication, in which pressure in the oil film carries part of the load, and the friction coefficient falls sharply. Increasing it further gives hydrodynamic lubrication, in which the oil film fully separates the surfaces; the friction coefficient passes its minimum and then rises gently because of the viscous resistance of the oil.

In hydrodynamic lubrication, oil is drawn toward the direction in which the gap between the sliding surfaces narrows like a wedge, and pressure develops there to support the load. This is called the wedge effect, and the higher the speed and viscosity, the thicker the oil film. Where contact pressures are very high, as in rolling bearings and gears, elastic deformation of the contact and the rise in oil viscosity with pressure come into play, giving elastohydrodynamic lubrication in which even an oil film thinner than 1 µm can separate the surfaces. The film thickness ratio, the ratio of film thickness to surface roughness, serves as a guide to the lubrication state.

A bearing operated slightly on the hydrodynamic side of the friction minimum keeps a stable friction coefficient even when speed or load changes. On the boundary side of the minimum, a temperature rise that lowers viscosity moves the bearing still closer to boundary lubrication, increasing friction and possibly leading to seizure. Starting and stopping always pass through boundary lubrication, so materials for rubbing surfaces must resist adhesion even when the oil film breaks. Oil additives, surface treatments and solid lubricants are used mainly to reduce friction and wear in this boundary lubrication region.

faq.q: What is boundary lubrication?
faq.a: It is a state in which the oil film has become very thin, asperities touch, and friction is governed by molecules adsorbed on the surfaces and thin films formed by reaction with additives. Oil viscosity has little effect, and the friction coefficient is about 0.1. It occurs at starting and stopping, and at low speed under heavy load.

faq.q: Does a more viscous oil always lower friction?
faq.a: Not necessarily. In the boundary and mixed lubrication regions the oil film thickens and friction falls, but once the bearing is already in the hydrodynamic region, viscous resistance increases and friction loss actually grows. This is why low-viscosity oils are used to save energy.

faq.q: Why can results be organized by the bearing characteristic number?
faq.a: Pressure in a hydrodynamic oil film grows in proportion to viscosity and speed and opposes the bearing pressure. The combination viscosity × speed ÷ pressure therefore expresses whether the oil film can carry the load. Experiments under different conditions can be collapsed onto a single curve using this number.

凝着摩耗.desc: Wear in which metals bond at the real contact spots and, as sliding shears the junctions, material transfers to the counterface or detaches. It causes seizure.

アブレシブ摩耗.desc: Wear in which hard particles or hard asperities on the counterface scratch and cut material from a softer surface. It drops greatly when the surface is made harder than the particles.

浸炭.desc: A treatment in which low-carbon steel is held in a carbon-bearing atmosphere in the austenite region to raise the carbon content of the surface layer. Quenching then turns the surface into hard martensite.

窒化処理.desc: A treatment in which steel is held in a nitrogen-bearing atmosphere below the A₁ transformation temperature to form hard nitrides in the surface layer. No quenching is needed and distortion is small.

無電解ニッケルめっき.desc: Plating in which nickel is deposited autocatalytically by a reducing agent without a power supply. The deposit contains phosphorus and forms a uniform thickness even on parts of complex shape.

網目形成酸化物.desc: An oxide such as SiO₂, B₂O₃ or P₂O₅ whose cations form oxygen polyhedra that share corners, building a glass network even on its own.

about.p: In 1932 Zachariasen proposed that an oxide forms glass readily when it can build a continuous network without long-range periodicity while keeping the same short-range bonding as the crystal. As conditions he named a small cation coordination number of 3 or 4, oxygen bonded to no more than two cations, polyhedra sharing only corners rather than edges or faces, and each polyhedron sharing at least three corners. SiO₂, B₂O₃, P₂O₅ and GeO₂ meet these conditions and form glass on their own.

Alkali and alkaline-earth oxides such as Na₂O, K₂O and CaO do not form glass by themselves; when they join the network, they break Si-O-Si bridges and create non-bridging oxygens. Their cations occupy interstices in the network, and these oxides are called network modifiers. Al₂O₃, ZnO, TiO₂ and the like are called intermediate oxides; they hardly form glass alone, but depending on composition they either join the network or modify it. For example, Al³⁺ whose charge is compensated by Na⁺ and the like enters the network as AlO₄ tetrahedra and reduces the number of non-bridging oxygens.

The more network formers and bridges a glass has, the higher its viscosity and glass transition temperature, the smaller its thermal expansion and the higher its chemical durability. Silica glass is the most fully connected glass and has excellent heat resistance, but shaping it requires very high temperatures. Soda-lime glass is a composition that lowers the forming temperature with Na₂O and restores durability with CaO. Borosilicate glass adds B₂O₃ to reduce thermal expansion and is used for laboratory ware and heat-resistant tableware. The proportions of formers and modifiers are chosen to suit the application.

faq.q: What kind of network does B₂O₃ form?
faq.a: In B₂O₃ glass, planar triangular BO₃ units, in which boron is bonded to three oxygens, share corners to form a network. Adding alkali converts some boron to fourfold-coordinated BO₄ tetrahedra, strengthening the network, so up to a certain composition property changes are not simple. This is called the boron anomaly.

faq.q: Is there a glass made only of a network former?
faq.a: Yes. Silica glass (fused silica), made of SiO₂ alone, is the classic example; its thermal expansion is very small and it transmits ultraviolet light well. Its viscosity is high, however, and melting and shaping it requires temperatures of about 2000 °C, so it is costly to make.

faq.q: Do metallic glasses have elements that play a role like network formers?
faq.a: Metallic glasses are held together by metallic bonding and have no directional network like oxide glasses. They become glass through a densely packed, disordered arrangement of atoms, and how readily they form depends on differences in atomic size and on the heat of mixing.

網目修飾酸化物.desc: An oxide such as Na₂O, K₂O or CaO that breaks bridges in a glass network to create non-bridging oxygens, with its cations occupying interstices in the network. It lowers the viscosity.

非架橋酸素.desc: An oxygen in a glass network bonded to only one network-forming cation and not linked to a neighboring polyhedron. It increases when modifying oxides are added.

強化ガラス.desc: Glass strengthened by quenching a heated sheet with air so that compressive stress remains at the surface and tensile stress inside. When it breaks, it shatters into small granules.

化学強化ガラス.desc: Glass strengthened by exchanging Na⁺ in its surface layer for larger K⁺ in a molten salt, introducing large compressive stress in the surface layer. It can be used even for thin sheets.

金属ガラス.desc: An amorphous alloy solidified from a metallic melt without crystallizing. With no dislocations, it has high strength and a large elastic strain limit. Thick pieces are called bulk metallic glasses.

about.p: Metallic melts have low viscosity and their atoms rearrange quickly, so they normally crystallize as soon as they are cooled. Since an amorphous alloy was first made in 1960 by quenching an Au-Si alloy at about 10⁶ K/s, early metallic glasses were ribbons a few tens of µm thick made by melt spinning, in which the melt is jetted onto a rotating copper wheel, and similar methods. From around 1990, multicomponent alloys based on Zr, Pd, Mg, Fe and others brought critical cooling rates down to about 1–100 K/s, and bulk metallic glasses from several mm to centimeter scale could be made simply by casting into a copper mold.

Metallic glasses have no dislocations or grain boundaries, so their yield strength is much higher than that of crystalline alloys of the same elements: about 1.8 GPa for Zr-based glasses, and over 5 GPa for some Co-based ones. Their Young's modulus is about 30% lower than that of crystals, and their elastic strain limit of about 2% is several times that of most crystalline metals. At room temperature, however, deformation concentrates in thin shear bands and there is no work hardening, so in tension they fracture with almost no elongation. To offset this brittleness, composites with dispersed crystalline phases and similar approaches are being studied.

about.h: Forming in the supercooled-liquid range, and uses
about.p: When a metallic glass is heated, it becomes a supercooled liquid of reduced viscosity above the glass transition temperature Tg and crystallizes at the higher crystallization temperature Tx. In the range between Tg and Tx it can deform greatly under small forces like a plastic, allowing precision forming that replicates fine mold features. Uses include springs, sporting goods and precision parts that exploit the large elastic energy, and Fe-based ribbons, which have no magnetocrystalline anisotropy and small coercivity, are used for low-loss transformer cores.

faq.q: Do metallic glasses crystallize over time?
faq.a: They are thermodynamically less stable than crystals, but at room temperature atoms barely move, so for practical purposes they do not crystallize. Held long near Tg, however, they can become brittle through structural relaxation or crystallize, so the service temperature is kept well below Tg.

faq.q: Are metallic glasses and amorphous alloys the same thing?
faq.a: Both refer to alloys without crystalline periodicity and are used almost interchangeably. Those that show a clear glass transition on heating and have a supercooled-liquid range are sometimes distinguished specifically as metallic glasses.

faq.q: Why do multicomponent alloys form glass more readily?
faq.a: When atoms of different sizes mix while attracting each other, the liquid takes a dense, disordered arrangement in which atoms move slowly, and forming crystals requires extensive rearrangement of atoms. A lower liquidus temperature, which raises the reduced glass transition temperature, also helps.

換算ガラス転移温度.desc: The glass transition temperature Tg divided by the liquidus temperature Tl, Trg = Tg/Tl. The larger it is, the more readily a melt forms glass, with about 2/3 or more taken as a guideline.

アモルファスシリコン.desc: Silicon without long-range periodicity. a-Si:H, with its dangling bonds terminated by hydrogen, is used in thin-film transistors and thin-film solar cells.
